> D. COMMUNICATION PROTOCOLS AND ALGORITHMS

Communication protocols and algorithms are fundamental to ensuring efficient and reliable data exchange in WSNs. These methods are designed to address the unique challenges of WSNs, including energy constraints, dynamic topology, and limited computational resources. This subsection explores Medium Access Control (MAC) and routing protocols, highlighting key operational principles [63]. 

> 1) MEDIUM ACCESS CONTROL PROTOCOLS

MAC protocols manage access to the shared communication medium, ensuring collision-free and energy-efficient data transmission. These protocols are vital in reducing idle listening and minimizing energy consumption. At a high level, they are classified into Contention-based, Contention-free (Synchronous, Asynchronous), and Hybrid. 

> a: CONTENTION-FREE

Several contention-free MAC protocols have been developed to enhance energy efficiency, reliability, and scalability in WSNs by eliminating collisions and minimizing retrans-missions. Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) assigns dedicated time slots to nodes, ensuring collision-free com-munication and reducing energy waste, making it particularly effective in clustered networks such as LEACH. Similarly, Frequency Division Multiple Access (FDMA) provides an alternative by allocating different frequency bands to nodes, allowing simultaneous transmissions while minimizing inter-ference. Unlike carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA), which relies on a shared channel and is prone to congestion and collisions, FDMA improves channel utilization and reduces retransmissions. However, its implementation requires precise frequency synchroniza-tion and more complex hardware, making it less suitable for energy-constrained WSNs than TDMA and hybrid approaches. Despite these challenges, FDMA is advanta-geous in applications that demand continuous, real-time data transmission, such as industrial automation and environmen-tal monitoring, where dedicated frequency channels enhance reliability and throughput. In modern WSNs, FDMA is often combined with TDMA or Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) to improve scalability and efficiency, particularly in large-scale deployments. Finally, among modern contention-free protocols, IEEE 802.15.4e TSCH (Time Slotted Channel Hopping) enhances reliability and mitigates interference through synchronized time slots and frequency [64]. 

> b: CONTENTION-BASED

Dense WSNs often rely on contention-based protocols such as CSMA/CA. However, these protocols face challenges like higher collision rates, particularly in high-density scenarios. To mitigate this, mechanisms such as RTS/CTS (Request to Send/Clear to Send) handshaking are employed to reduce packet collisions and improve transmission reliability [65], [66]. Contention-based MAC protocols can be broadly classi-fied into synchronous and asynchronous approaches. Syn-chronous MAC protocols, such as Sensor-MAC (S-MAC) and Timeout-MAC (T-MAC), employ periodic sleep/wake cycles to conserve energy. T-MAC optimizes energy effi-ciency by dynamically adjusting active periods based on net-work traffic conditions, reducing latency during high-traffic periods at the cost of slightly increased energy consumption. Also, dynamic MAC (DMAC) adjusts duty cycling based on traffic patterns, ensuring adaptive power management [67], [68]. In synchronous MAC protocols, nodes alternate between active and sleep states in synchronized cycles, where the frame time Tframe is given by Tframe = Tlisten + Tsleep ,where Tlisten and Tsleep denote the listening and sleeping durations, respectively [69], [70]. Unlike synchronous approaches, asynchronous MAC protocols operate without global synchronization, allow- 

> 96372 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. Trigka, E. Dritsas: WSNs: From Fundamentals and Applications to Innovations and Future Trends

ing nodes to follow independent schedules. This enables flexible duty cycling, reducing idle listening and energy waste. WiseMAC, for example, minimizes idle listening by allowing the nodes to wake up only when a transmission is expected, using preamble sampling. Several asynchronous MAC protocols have been developed to optimize energy efficiency further. X-MAC is designed as an enhancement over Berkeley MAC (B-MAC), improving preamble handling by shortening preambles and enabling early acknowledg-ment. Receiver-Initiated MAC (RI-MAC) shifts transmission initiation to the receiver, reducing idle listening. B-MAC employs Low-Power Listening (LPL) and adaptive preamble sampling to balance energy efficiency and latency. These and other asynchronous protocols enhance adaptability and energy conservation in low-duty-cycle WSN applications by reducing unnecessary transmissions and improving medium access efficiency [71]. 

> c: HYBRID

Hybrid protocols, such as Zebra-MAC (Z-MAC), adaptively switch between contention-based access under low traffic and TDMA-based scheduling when congestion increases, improving efficiency. More advanced approaches integrate cross-layer optimization to improve performance further. 

> d: ADAPTIVE

Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based MAC proto-cols [72] have gained attention for their ability to dynamically learn optimal transmission strategies by adapting to changing network conditions. These approaches leverage deep RL techniques to optimize channel access, minimize collisions, and improve energy efficiency without relying on predefined scheduling rules. By leveraging these alternative MAC protocols, WSNs can achieve better energy conservation, reduced latency, and increased robustness, depending on application-specific requirements. > 2) ROUTING PROTOCOLS

Routing protocols in WSNs play a crucial role in determining efficient paths for data transmission from sensor nodes to the sink while considering energy constraints, scalability, mobil-ity, and security. Selecting a suitable routing protocol depends on the network topology, communication requirements, and operational constraints. Various routing protocols have been proposed. These protocols are designed to minimize energy consumption, ensure reliability, and balance traffic loads [74]. The following paragraphs are categorized based on their key objectives and techniques. 

> a: DATA-CENTRIC

Data-centric routing protocols enhance energy efficiency in WSNs by minimizing redundant transmissions through in-network aggregation and interest-driven forwarding. Unlike traditional address-centric approaches, they employ a query-response mechanism to retrieve relevant data, dynamically adjusting transmission paths and eliminating unnecessary messages. These capabilities make data-centric protocols particularly effective for applications requiring prolonged network operation under energy constraints. One of the fundamental characteristics of data-centric routing is its ability to employ interest propagation and data aggregation to optimize communication efficiency. The sink node broadcasts an interest query to initiate data collection. Nodes that contain relevant information respond by forwarding their data along optimized paths, where intermediate nodes aggregate similar data before relaying it further. This aggregation process minimizes redundant packet transmissions, reduces congestion, and conserves energy. The total energy consumption in data-centric routing protocols can be expressed as 

Edata-centric = Equery + Eforwarding + Eaggregation

Directed Diffusion (DD) [77] is a well-known example that employs reinforcement-based path selection. It propagates interest messages from the sink node to establish data gra-dients, guiding packets through optimized paths. Similarly, Rumor Routing (RR) minimizes query flooding by deploying long-lived agents that traverse the network to disseminate event information. Another approach, COUGAR, introduces a query-processing layer that integrates data from multiple sources, optimizing the overall communication overhead. In addition to Rumor and COUGAR, several other proto-cols enhance data dissemination and adaptability in WSNs. Sensor Protocols for Information via Negotiation (SPIN) minimizes redundant transmissions through negotiation, while Gradient-Based Routing (GBR) employs hop-based gradient routing for efficient data forwarding. Moreover, Constrained Anisotropic Diffusion Routing (CADR) dynam-ically adjusts data propagation to balance network load,

> b: HIERARCHICAL (CLUSTER-BASED)

LEACH [81], [82] is one of the most widely used protocols, periodically selecting new CHs to distribute energy consumption across the network evenly. Power Efficient Adaptive Clustering Hierarchy (PEACH) enables adaptive clustering formation without requiring explicit control messages, reducing overhead and improving energy efficiency. Unlike traditional clustering schemes, PEACH leverages overheard packets to dynamically form clusters, making it particularly effective in environments with unpredictable topology changes. Power-Efficient GAthering in Sensor Information System (PEGASIS) organizes sensor nodes into a chain-based topology, where each node transmits data to its nearest neighbor in a sequential manner until reaching a designated leader node, which aggregates the col-lected data and transmits it to the sink. This approach reduces the number of direct transmissions to the sink, minimizes long-distance communication, significantly lowers energy consumption, and balances network lifetime by distributing the communication load among nodes over multiple rounds. Moreover, threshold-sensitive Energy Efficient Network (TEEN) is tailored for time-critical applications by introduc-ing hard and soft thresholds, which control event-driven data transmission. Adaptive TEEN (APTEEN) extends TEEN by incorporating both periodic and event-driven communication, making it more flexible for diverse applications [83]. Meanwhile, Hybrid Energy-Efficient Distributed Clustering (HEED) improves CH selection by considering residual energy and node proximity, ensuring a balanced energy distribution and prolonged network lifetime [84]. These protocols continue to evolve, addressing the chal-lenges of scalability, mobility, and energy constraints in large-scale WSN deployments. > III. APPLICATIONS OF WIRELESS SENSOR NETWORKS

WSNs have emerged as transformative technologies across a broad spectrum of domains, leveraging distributed sensing, real-time data processing, and adaptive communication to address complex challenges. Their applications span diverse fields such as environmental monitoring, healthcare, indus-trial automation, smart cities, precision agriculture, disaster management and emergency response, energy management and renewable energy systems, transportation and logis-tics, aquatic and underwater monitoring, space exploration and planetary research, UAVs, and military defence. This section presents a detailed examination of their applications, emphasizing scientific advancements and domain-specific methodologies. 

> A. ENVIRONMENTAL MONITORING

WSNs are fundamental to environmental monitoring due to their capability to collect high-resolution spatiotemporal data from remote and hazardous areas. They are employed for applications like microclimate monitoring, pollutant detection, and disaster prediction [128]. For instance, microclimate monitoring utilizes tempera-ture, humidity, and solar radiation sensors to model localized weather patterns. Predictive algorithms such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) analyze the temporal dynamics of these parameters, enhancing forecasting accuracy. Pollution monitoring systems deploy gas sensors to measure concen-trations of NO 2, CO 2, and particulates, refining their outputs using Bayesian estimation to address sensor inaccuracies caused by environmental drift [129], [130]. In disaster prediction, WSNs play a pivotal role in early warning systems. For example, in landslide detection, pres-sure and soil moisture sensors are integrated into a distributed network. Data fusion techniques like distributed Kalman filtering combine sensor outputs to predict slope instability. Similarly, flood monitoring networks use ultrasonic and pressure sensors to measure water levels, employing adaptive routing protocols to maintain connectivity even during infrastructural damage [131], [132], [133]. 

> B. HEALTHCARE AND BIOMEDICAL APPLICATIONS

WSNs have revolutionized patient care and medical diagnos-tics in healthcare through real-time monitoring and predictive analysis. Body Sensor Networks (BSNs), a specialized WSN application, enable continuous tracking of physiological parameters such as electrocardiograph (ECG), SpO 2, and glucose levels [134]. Advanced applications include early detection of critical health events using AI-powered analysis. > IV. INNOVATIONS IN WSN TECHNOLOGIES

Breakthroughs in energy systems, communication protocols, data processing frameworks, and integration with emerging paradigms such as the IoT and AI have propelled WSNs’ evolution. > A. ENERGY HARVESTING AND AUTONOMOUS POWER MANAGEMENT

Energy availability is a defining constraint for WSNs. Innovations in energy harvesting technologies have shifted the paradigm from battery dependency to autonomous power systems. Solar cells remain the most mature technology, with advancements in Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithms improving efficiency under variable light conditions. For industrial environments, piezoelectric systems harvest vibrational energy from machinery, while Thermoelectric Generators (TEGs) utilize temperature gra-dients in high-heat regions such as manufacturing plants or engines [207], [208], [209]. Complementing these harvesting methods, ultra-low-power design principles in hardware and software ensure minimal energy wastage. Dynamic power scaling, duty-cycling mechanisms, and wake-up radios are now standard for managing operational energy. For instance, wake-up radios maintain nodes in a low-power state and activate them only upon detecting relevant communication signals, reducing idle listening [210], [211].

> V. CHALLENGES IN WSN APPLICATIONS

WSNs face numerous challenges that constrain their perfor-mance, scalability, and reliability. These issues arise from the inherent resource limitations of sensor nodes, dynamic deployment environments, and the increasing complexity of modern applications. Addressing these challenges requires a scientific understanding of their root causes and the development of targeted solutions. This section provides a detailed analysis of the technical and operational barriers to WSN deployment and functionality. Many of the challenges discussed in this section have been recognized since the early development of WSNs. However, they remain critical today, hindering system scalability, energy autonomy, and long-term reliability in real-world deployments. Their persistence, despite continu-ous innovation, highlights the need for renewed focus and interdisciplinary solutions tailored to emerging application contexts. 

> A. ENERGY LIMITATIONS AND DYNAMIC POWER OPTIMIZATION

Energy availability remains the most critical challenge in WSNs, directly affecting the longevity and functionality of deployments. Despite advancements in energy harvesting systems, their performance depends on environmental condi-tions, such as light availability for solar cells or temperature gradients for TEGs. This dependency introduces variability in energy supply, complicating power management in dynamic environments [267], [268]. Dynamic power optimization techniques attempt to address these limitations by adapting node operations based on real-time energy levels and task requirements. For example, stochastic models predict energy availability in hybrid harvesting systems, allowing nodes to adjust their duty cycles and communication schedules dynamically. How-ever, implementing these techniques requires computational resources, which further strain node energy reserves. Future research must focus on lightweight algorithms that balance computational overhead with power-saving benefits [269], [270], [271]. 

> B. NETWORK SCALABILITY AND CONGESTION CONTROL

Scaling WSNs to larger deployments introduces significant challenges in maintaining efficient communication and data processing. As the number of nodes increases, the network experiences higher congestion levels, packet collisions, and delays. Hierarchical clustering and tree-based routing protocols alleviate these issues by organizing nodes into manageable sub-networks, but they often require centralized control, which creates bottlenecks near the sink [272], [273]. Advanced approaches, such as adaptive clustering, utilize ML models to optimize cluster formation dynamically based on traffic patterns and energy levels. Additionally, cross-layer optimization techniques align routing, MAC protocols, and transport layers to reduce congestion holistically. These methods, while promising, demand computational and mem-ory resources that many sensor nodes lack [274], [275], [276]. 

> C. ENVIRONMENTAL INTERFERENCE AND DEPLOYMENT RESILIENCE

WSNs often operate in environments with fluctuating conditions, such as industrial sites with electromagnetic interference or underwater systems with high signal atten-uation. Environmental factors degrade communication links and sensor accuracy, necessitating robust error correction and reconfiguration mechanisms [277], [278]. Deployment resilience relies on redundancy and self-healing algorithms that reroute traffic and redistribute tasks among operational nodes during failures. For instance, network coding techniques improve data recovery by encod-ing transmitted packets, reducing the impact of packet loss. Furthermore, autonomous deployment strategies using UAVs extend network coverage and address node placement inaccuracies, but their real-time integration with existing WSNs remains an area of active research [279], [280], [281]. 

> D. SECURITY VULNERABILITIES IN RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED NODES

WSNs’ decentralized architecture, combined with their reliance on wireless communication, makes them vulnerable to a wide array of attacks, including eavesdropping, jamming, and sinkhole attacks. Conventional security solutions, such as public-key cryptography, are often unsuitable for WSNs due to their high computational and energy costs. Emerging lightweight cryptographic algorithms, such as ChaCha20 and SPECK, offer energy-efficient alternatives for encryption and authentication in resource-constrained WSN nodes [282], [283]. Additionally, blockchain-based distributed trust mech-anisms are being explored to secure decentralized WSN deployments [284], [285]. These mechanisms typically rely

> E. APPLICATION-AWARE SECURITY AND PRIVACY CONSIDERATIONS

The application domain strongly influences security and privacy challenges in WSNs. In healthcare, where WSNs support applications such as body sensor networks and remote monitoring, the sensitivity of collected physiological data demands privacy protection beyond secure transmission alone. Unauthorized access or inference attacks on patient data can have profound ethical and legal implications, especially under regulatory frameworks like HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) and GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation). Systems must balance responsiveness with privacy-preserving features such as data anonymization, selective data disclosure, and secure user authentication, without exceeding medical sensor nodes’ energy and processing limitations [288]. Similarly, in smart homes, behavioral data captured by sensor nodes poses privacy risks such as unauthorized surveil-lance and profiling if not adequately protected. In industrial automation, WSNs face cyber-physical threats including false data injection, actuator compromise, and availability-targeted attacks, which may disrupt safety-critical systems. These domain-specific risks underscore the importance of implementing security strategies that are both resource-aware and application-context sensitive [289].

As WSNs are deployed in increasingly dynamic and het-erogeneous environments, communication protocols must evolve to become intelligent and context-aware. The inte-gration of ML at the protocol level will enable adaptive mechanisms that adjust transmission power, routing paths, and frequency bands based on network conditions and application demands [316], [317].

Protocols leveraging RL can optimize multi-hop communication in large-scale deployments, addressing chal-lenges such as the energy hole problem and maintaining connectivity under high node density [318], [319], [320]. 

C. COLLABORATIVE AND FEDERATED INTELLIGENCE 

The future of WSNs lies in collaborative intelligence, where sensor nodes work together to analyze and interpret data, moving beyond simple data aggregation. FL, a decentralized approach to ML, allows nodes to train models while retaining their local data collaboratively. This approach not only reduces the communication overhead but also ensures data privacy, making it suitable for sensitive applications like healthcare and defense [321], [322]. Research is needed to optimize FL algorithms for resource-constrained WSNs. Techniques such as sparsification, quanti-zation, and model compression can reduce the computational and communication costs associated with collaborative intelligence. Furthermore, integrating edge servers to act as intermediaries between nodes and cloud systems will enhance scalability and processing capabilities [323], [324], [325]. 

D. QUANTUM SENSING AND COMMUNICATION 

Quantum technologies hold significant potential for advanc-ing the capabilities of WSNs. Quantum sensors, leveraging phenomena such as quantum entanglement and superposi-tion, offer unprecedented sensitivity and accuracy in detect-ing physical parameters like magnetic fields, temperature, and gravitational waves. These sensors could transform applications in environmental monitoring, healthcare, and space exploration [326], [327], [328]. Quantum communication protocols, such as Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), promise unbreakable security by utilizing the principles of quantum mechanics to detect eavesdropping. Future WSNs could integrate quantum com-munication technologies to safeguard critical data transmis-sions, particularly in defense and infrastructure monitoring applications [329], [330].

While quantum technologies offer significant potential, their integration into WSNs remains a long-term goal. Current quantum communication systems are not yet minia-turized or energy-efficient enough to meet the stringent constraints of typical sensor nodes. Most advancements are still at the experimental stage or limited to high-end applications. Progress in integrated quantum circuits and photonics may eventually enable compact quantum modules suitable for specialized WSN deployments. 

> E. BIO-INSPIRED AND SELF-ADAPTIVE ARCHITECTURES

Bio-inspired architectures, modeled after biological systems, are emerging as a promising approach to designing resilient and efficient WSNs. Techniques such as swarm intelligence, genetic algorithms, and neural-inspired learning mechanisms allow networks to adapt dynamically to environmental changes and node failures [331], [332]. For example, swarm intelligence algorithms mimic the collective behavior of social insects to optimize routing paths and resource allocation in large-scale WSNs. Neural-inspired architectures enable nodes to process sensory inputs and adapt their operations based on local observations, improving fault tolerance and reducing energy consumption. These self-adaptive systems will play a crucial role in ensuring network longevity and robustness in unpredictable environments [333], [334]. 

> F. WSNs IN EXTREME ENVIRONMENTS

Expanding the application of WSNs to extreme environments —such as deep oceans, polar regions, and outer space— presents unique challenges that require innovative solutions. Underwater WSNs, for instance, face high latency and limited bandwidth due to acoustic communication. Research into hybrid communication methods, combining acoustic, optical, and radio frequency technologies, aims to overcome these limitations [335], [336], [337]. In space exploration, WSNs must operate autonomously under extreme radiation and temperature variations. Radiation-hardened hardware and fault-tolerant algorithms will be critical for ensuring reliability. Additionally, lightweight protocols for interplanetary communication are necessary to enable real-time data exchange between planetary sensor networks and orbital spacecraft [338], [339], [340]. 

> G. INTEGRATION WITH DIGITAL TWINS

Digital Twins, virtual replicas of physical systems, are poised to revolutionize WSN applications by enabling advanced simulations, predictive analytics, and real-time monitoring. WSNs will serve as the primary data acquisition layer for Digital Twins, continuously feeding them with real-world observations [341], [342]. Future research will focus on seamless integration between WSNs and Digital Twins, emphasizing low-latency commu-nication and data consistency. For example, in smart city management, Digital Twins could simulate the impact of policy changes on traffic flow or energy consumption using real-time data from WSNs. Ensuring synchronization and scalability in these integrated systems will be key to their success [343], [344]. 

> H. SECURITY AND PRIVACY IN EMERGING APPLICATIONS

As WSNs expand into applications involving sensitive data, such as personalized healthcare and smart infrastructure, ensuring security and privacy will become increasingly important. Future research will explore advanced cryp-tographic techniques, such as homomorphic encryption, which allows data to be processed without being decrypted, preserving privacy while enabling analytics [345], [346], [347]. Decentralized security frameworks like blockchain-based authentication and access control will also gain traction. These systems will eliminate single points of failure and enhance trust in multi-vendor deployments. Moreover, anomaly detection systems leveraging deep learning will identify security breaches in real time, reducing the response time to cyberattacks [348], [349], [350]. 

> I. MULTI-MODAL AND MULTI-SENSOR FUSION

The integration of multi-modal sensing in WSNs enables richer datasets and more comprehensive analyses. Future trends will focus on efficient fusion techniques that combine data from heterogeneous sensors, such as image, acoustic, and environmental sensors, to improve decision-making accuracy [351], [352]. For instance, in precision agriculture, data from soil moisture sensors, drones, and weather stations can be combined using fusion algorithms to optimize irrigation and pest control. In healthcare, integrating physiological signals like ECG, SpO 2, and motion data will enhance diagnostic precision. Research into lightweight and real-time fusion algorithms will be crucial for extending these capabilities to resource-constrained WSNs [353], [354], [355]. VII. CONCLUSION 

WSNs have emerged as a cornerstone of modern technology, addressing critical challenges across diverse domains such as environmental monitoring, healthcare, industrial automation, and beyond. The advancements in energy harvesting, commu-nication protocols, and data processing have enabled WSNs to transcend traditional limitations, offering scalable, reliable, and efficient solutions. However, the ever-expanding scope of WSN applications brings with it complex challenges and emerging research gaps that demand innovative approaches. One of the central themes in the evolution of WSNs is achieving sustainability through energy efficiency and self-sustaining systems. Innovations such as multi-source energy harvesting and dynamic power management algorithms represent significant strides toward prolonging network lifespans, particularly in remote and resource-constrained environments. These developments ensure that WSNs can maintain functionality in diverse settings, from dense urban areas to extreme environments. Integrating WSNs with emerging paradigms such as IoT, AI, and digital twins highlights their pivotal role in shaping future technologies. Adopting intelligent protocols and collaborative processing frameworks has transformed WSNs into data collection networks and platforms for real-time analytics and autonomous decision-making. FL and edge intelligence exemplify the potential for distributed processing, ensuring that WSNs remain viable even in

Scalability issues in dense networks, dynamic topology management, and robust security are persistent obstacles that must be addressed through cutting-edge research. Security, in particular, remains a significant concern, as WSNs are inherently vulnerable to attacks due to their resource constraints. Developing lightweight cryptographic methods and blockchain-based trust mechanisms is essential for safeguarding sensitive data in applications such as healthcare, defense, and industrial automation. Similarly, quantum communication and bio-inspired architectures are set to redefine the boundaries of what WSNs can achieve regarding reliability and adaptability. This study contributes a concise review of the current landscape of WSNs, structured around three dimensions: (i) domain-specific applications, (ii) technological innovations such as energy-aware and AI-integrated systems, and (iii) challenge-driven analysis across areas including energy effi-ciency, scalability, and security. Furthermore, comparative and case-based tabular summaries are presented to bridge theoretical advancements with real-world implementations. Future research should prioritize the development of hybrid energy harvesting models with adaptive power scheduling, lightweight and context-sensitive security proto-cols, and resilient WSN frameworks capable of autonomous reconfiguration in extreme environments such as underwater, polar, and space missions. In parallel, optimized 5G-enabled architectures, fog-assisted intelligence, and seamless interoperability must be advanced to enhance real-time data processing and reduce latency. Cross-domain integration with Digital Twins, FL, and self-organizing systems will be critical to realizing the full potential of next-generation WSNs. The trajectory of WSN development underscores their potential as transformative enablers across scientific, indus-trial, and societal domains. By addressing these open challenges and embracing interdisciplinary collaboration, WSNs are poised to become integral to the next wave of technological innovation across both Earth-bound and remote environments.

# Wireless Sensor Networks: From Fundamentals and Applications to Innovations and Future Trends 

MARIA TRIGKA  AND ELIAS DRITSAS 

> Department of Informatics and Computer Engineering, University of West Attica, Egaleo Park Campus, 122 43 Athens, Greece

Corresponding author: Maria Trigka (mtrigka@uniwa.gr) The publication of the article in OA mode was financially supported by HEAL-Link. 

ABSTRACT Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) have transformed data acquisition and processing across diverse domains such as environmental monitoring, healthcare, and industrial automation. Recent advancements in areas such as federated intelligence, blockchain-based trust mechanisms, and quantum sensing are reshaping the landscape of WSNs. Yet, their full implications for next-generation applications demand deeper exploration. This survey is driven by the need to synthesize these emerging directions through a forward-looking and interdisciplinary lens, highlighting their transformative potential in evolving WSNs into intelligent, autonomous systems. It examines key solutions in energy harvesting, adaptive communication, and edge intelligence, which address persistent constraints like limited energy availability, dynamic topologies, and scalability. Moreover, it highlights the integration of WSNs with disruptive technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and digital twins, enabling intelligent, autonomous systems capable of real-time analytics. Critical energy optimization, security, and data management challenges are explored alongside cutting-edge solutions like federated learning (FL), quantum sensing, and blockchain-based trust mechanisms. Future research directions emphasize bio-inspired architectures, hybrid communication in extreme environments, and efficient multi-modal data fusion. This survey serves as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to design resilient, intelligent WSN-based systems for the next generation of applications. 

INDEX TERMS Wireless sensor networks, adaptive communication protocols, Internet of Things, smart systems, data processing. 

I. INTRODUCTION 

WSNs have emerged as a transformative technology for distributed sensing, data collection, and communication in diverse applications ranging from environmental monitoring to industrial automation. Comprising spatially distributed sensor nodes capable of sensing, processing, and commu-nicating, WSNs represent a paradigm shift in how data is captured, processed, and acted upon. The ability of these networks to operate autonomously in dynamic and resource-constrained environments has made them indispens-able in addressing complex scientific, industrial, and societal challenges [1].

> II. KEY COMPONENTS AND TECHNOLOGIES IN WIRELESS SENSOR NETWORKS

WSNs operate on an intricate framework of architectures, algorithms, and mathematical techniques, each tailored to optimize system efficiency, reliability, and scalability. This section delves into the fundamental components and technologies that maintain modern WSNs, emphasizing architectural designs, communication methodologies, and parameter estimation techniques. 

> A. ARCHITECTURAL MODELS IN WSNs

Sensor node architecture is the backbone of WSNs, defining the system’s operational capabilities, energy efficiency, and scalability. It comprises multiple interconnected subsystems, including sensing, processing, communication, and power management. Modern sensor node architectures have evolved to address the specific challenges of WSN environments, including resource constraints, network scalability, and oper-ational longevity. This subsection explores the nuances of different architectures (single-tier and multi-tier, centralized, decentralized, and distributed, and duty-cycled), emphasizing their design principles, performance characteristics, and application contexts [14], [15]. 

> 1) SINGLE-TIER AND MULTI-TIER ARCHITECTURES

Single-tier architectures represent a foundational approach in WSN design, where each sensor node is identical in functionality and performs all tasks independently. Nodes in this architecture sense environmental data, process it locally, and communicate it to a sink or base station. This uniformity simplifies network design and deployment, making single-tier architectures suitable for small-scale or static applications where uniform sensing is sufficient [16]. However, single-tier architectures often suffer from scala-bility and energy inefficiency. Nodes closer to the sink bear a higher communication burden due to their role in relaying data from distant nodes, leading to rapid energy depletion in these critical nodes and potentially causing network partition-ing [17]. Despite these challenges, single-tier architectures are widely adopted for applications requiring uniform data collection, such as indoor environmental monitoring, where simplicity and cost-effectiveness are prioritized over scalability [18], [19]. Multi-tier architectures introduce a hierarchical structure that mitigates the limitations of single-tier systems by assigning specialized roles to different nodes based on their capabilities and positions. In a typical multi-tier design, lower-tier nodes focus on local data collection and trans-mission to higher-tier nodes, which aggregate and process the data before forwarding it to the sink. This arrangement significantly reduces communication overhead for lower-tier nodes, extending their operational lifespan and enhancing the overall network efficiency [20], [21]. Multi-tier architectures outperform in scalability, as their hierarchical organization minimizes redundant communica-tion and localizes processing tasks. They also enhance fault tolerance, as higher-tier nodes can dynamically redistribute roles among themselves in the event of node failure. Despite these advantages, the complexity of clustering algorithms, role assignment, and inter-tier synchronization adds to the design and operational overhead. Applications such as smart city infrastructure and industrial automation benefit significantly from multi-tier architectures, as they can support diverse sensing requirements while maintaining energy efficiency and robustness [22], [23]. 

> 2) CENTRALIZED, DECENTRALIZED, AND DISTRIBUTED ARCHITECTURES

The architectural paradigm of a WSN plays a decisive role in determining its scalability, reliability, and energy efficiency. Depending on how tasks such as data aggregation, decision-making, and control are distributed among nodes, WSN architectures are broadly categorized into centralized, decentralized, and distributed models. Each architecture has distinct operational characteristics, trade-offs, and suitability

a: CENTRALIZED ARCHITECTURES 

A single control point characterizes centralized architectures, typically a sink or base station, that performs data aggrega-tion, processing, and decision-making for the entire network. In this model, all sensor nodes transmit their collected data directly or indirectly to the sink, which acts as the computational hub. This arrangement simplifies the design and implementation of the network, as the sink has a global view of the data and can execute complex computational tasks that individual sensor nodes cannot perform [25], [26], [27]. The primary advantage of centralized architectures is the ease of implementing sophisticated data analytics and optimization algorithms at the sink. This capability makes them highly effective for applications requiring intensive data processing, such as environmental modeling or industrial diagnostics. However, centralized architectures suffer from significant limitations, including the potential for bottlenecks at the sink and the lack of fault tolerance. Since all nodes transmit directly to a single sink, the failure of that central node can result in complete network disruption. Furthermore, communication range and power requirements increase for nodes located farther from the sink. This can result in uneven energy consumption across the network and early depletion of distant nodes, ultimately limiting the overall network lifetime [28], [29].

Applications of centralized architectures are typically found in small-scale or static deployments where network scalability and redundancy are not primary concerns. For instance, greenhouse monitoring systems often adopt acentralized design, as the spatial constraints and low node density make this approach efficient [30]. 

> b: DECENTRALIZED ARCHITECTURES

Decentralized architectures mitigate the drawbacks of cen-tralized systems by introducing hierarchical structures that distribute computational and communication tasks across multiple nodes. This model organizes sensor nodes into clusters, each managed by a cluster head (CH). The CH aggregates data from its member nodes, processes it locally, and forwards the results to the sink or higher-tier nodes. This hierarchical design reduces the communication overhead and energy consumption for individual sensor nodes, particularly those in lower tiers [31], [32]. Decentralized architectures excel in scalability and fault tolerance. By distributing roles and responsibilities, they prevent the formation of single points of failure and can reconfigure dynamically in response to node failures or changes in network topology. These features make decen-tralized architectures ideal for applications in smart cities, precision agriculture, and industrial automation, where the network must adapt to variable conditions and maintain consistent performance [33], [34]. Despite their advantages, decentralized architectures intro-duce challenges related to cluster formation, CH selection, and inter-cluster synchronization. Low-Energy Adaptive Clustering Hierarchy (LEACH) is widely used as it was one of the first protocols to introduce clustering in WSNs. However, it employs a basic clustering mechanism with random CH selection. It lacks advanced features such as adaptive decision-making, multi-hop communication, and energy-aware optimization, making it less efficient than more sophisticated approaches (detailed in the routing protocols section) that balance energy efficiency with network perfor-mance [35]. While decentralized and multi-tier architectures originate from different perspectives (namely, protocol-level organi-zation versus system-level hierarchy), they are structurally aligned. Both arrange sensor nodes into hierarchical layers, where lower-tier nodes communicate with coordinating entities termed CHs in decentralized systems and higher-tier nodes in multi-tier designs. These coordinators handle data aggregation and forwarding, reducing communication overhead and enhancing scalability. Despite the varied terminology, the roles and communication patterns are functionally equivalent, allowing for unified modeling in energy and performance analysis. 

> c: DISTRIBUTED ARCHITECTURES

Distributed architectures represent the most decentral-ized form of WSN design, where all sensor nodes collaboratively participate in data aggregation, processing, and decision-making without relying on a single con-trol point or hierarchical structure. Each node operates autonomously, making local decisions based on observations and interactions with neighbouring nodes. This peer-to-peer design offers unparalleled scalability and fault tolerance, as the failure of individual nodes does not compromise the network’s overall functionality [36], [37]. The distributed nature of this architecture relies heavily on consensus algorithms to synchronize decisions across the network. A typical example is the average consensus algorithm, which computes a global parameter, such as the average temperature, based on local observations. In this paradigm, energy consumption is minimized by limiting node activity to essential operations such as sensing, computation, and communication, while maximizing low-power sleep dura-tions during idle periods. > B. DATA AGGREGATION AND RELIABILITY MECHANISMS

Data aggregation techniques reduce communication over-head by combining data from multiple sensor nodes before transmission, minimizing redundancy and improving energy efficiency. This process is particularly beneficial in environmental monitoring, precision agriculture, and structural health monitoring applications, where distributed sensors generate large volumes of similar or correlated data. By aggregating data at intermediate nodes, the packets transmitted across the network are significantly reduced, leading to lower energy consumption and extended network lifetime. Several aggregation techniques have been proposed to optimize data fusion and minimize redundant transmissions. Hierarchical aggregation organizes nodes into clusters where a designated CH collects and processes data before for-warding it to the sink. Tree-based aggregation constructs a hierarchical routing tree where intermediate nodes perform iterative aggregation as data is relayed toward the sink, reducing redundant transmissions [49]. Adaptive aggregation mechanisms adjust the aggregation level dynamically based on network conditions, ensuring trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. Despite its benefits, data aggregation introduces challenges such as increased processing delay, data integrity risks, and compromised security, as aggregating nodes may become targets for adversarial attacks. Secure aggregation tech-niques [50] leveraging homomorphic encryption, lightweight and cryptographic methods have been developed to mitigate these risks while preserving efficiency. Error control mechanisms ensure data integrity during transmission by addressing issues such as interference and packet loss. Forward Error Correction (FEC) adds redundant data to packets, enabling receivers to correct certain errors without requiring retransmission [51]. The trade-off involves increased computational energy for encoding and decoding. Alternatively, Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) relies on retransmitting corrupted packets, increasing reliability at the expense of additional communication energy [52], [53]. > D. COMMUNICATION PROTOCOLS AND ALGORITHMS

Communication protocols and algorithms are fundamental to ensuring efficient and reliable data exchange in WSNs. These methods are designed to address the unique challenges of WSNs, including energy constraints, dynamic topology, and limited computational resources. This subsection explores Medium Access Control (MAC) and routing protocols, highlighting key operational principles [63]. 

> 1) MEDIUM ACCESS CONTROL PROTOCOLS

MAC protocols manage access to the shared communication medium, ensuring collision-free and energy-efficient data transmission. These protocols are vital in reducing idle listening and minimizing energy consumption. At a high level, they are classified into Contention-based, Contention-free (Synchronous, Asynchronous), and Hybrid. 

> a: CONTENTION-FREE

Several contention-free MAC protocols have been developed to enhance energy efficiency, reliability, and scalability in WSNs by eliminating collisions and minimizing retrans-missions. Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) assigns dedicated time slots to nodes, ensuring collision-free com-munication and reducing energy waste, making it particularly effective in clustered networks such as LEACH. Similarly, Frequency Division Multiple Access (FDMA) provides an alternative by allocating different frequency bands to nodes, allowing simultaneous transmissions while minimizing inter-ference. Unlike carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA), which relies on a shared channel and is prone to congestion and collisions, FDMA improves channel utilization and reduces retransmissions. However, its implementation requires precise frequency synchroniza-tion and more complex hardware, making it less suitable for energy-constrained WSNs than TDMA and hybrid approaches. Despite these challenges, FDMA is advanta-geous in applications that demand continuous, real-time data transmission, such as industrial automation and environmen-tal monitoring, where dedicated frequency channels enhance reliability and throughput. In modern WSNs, FDMA is often combined with TDMA or Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) to improve scalability and efficiency, particularly in large-scale deployments. Finally, among modern contention-free protocols, IEEE 802.15.4e TSCH (Time Slotted Channel Hopping) enhances reliability and mitigates interference through synchronized time slots and frequency [64]. 

> b: CONTENTION-BASED

Dense WSNs often rely on contention-based protocols such as CSMA/CA. However, these protocols face challenges like higher collision rates, particularly in high-density scenarios. To mitigate this, mechanisms such as RTS/CTS (Request to Send/Clear to Send) handshaking are employed to reduce packet collisions and improve transmission reliability [65], [66]. Contention-based MAC protocols can be broadly classi-fied into synchronous and asynchronous approaches. Syn-chronous MAC protocols, such as Sensor-MAC (S-MAC) and Timeout-MAC (T-MAC), employ periodic sleep/wake cycles to conserve energy. T-MAC optimizes energy effi-ciency by dynamically adjusting active periods based on net-work traffic conditions, reducing latency during high-traffic periods at the cost of slightly increased energy consumption. Also, dynamic MAC (DMAC) adjusts duty cycling based on traffic patterns, ensuring adaptive power management [67], [68]. In synchronous MAC protocols, nodes alternate between active and sleep states in synchronized cycles, where the frame time Tframe is given by Tframe = Tlisten + Tsleep ,where Tlisten and Tsleep denote the listening and sleeping durations, respectively [69], [70]. Unlike synchronous approaches, asynchronous MAC protocols operate without global synchronization, allow- 

> 96372 VOLUME 13, 2025 M. Trigka, E. Dritsas: WSNs: From Fundamentals and Applications to Innovations and Future Trends

ing nodes to follow independent schedules. This enables flexible duty cycling, reducing idle listening and energy waste. WiseMAC, for example, minimizes idle listening by allowing the nodes to wake up only when a transmission is expected, using preamble sampling. Several asynchronous MAC protocols have been developed to optimize energy efficiency further. X-MAC is designed as an enhancement over Berkeley MAC (B-MAC), improving preamble handling by shortening preambles and enabling early acknowledg-ment. Receiver-Initiated MAC (RI-MAC) shifts transmission initiation to the receiver, reducing idle listening. B-MAC employs Low-Power Listening (LPL) and adaptive preamble sampling to balance energy efficiency and latency. These and other asynchronous protocols enhance adaptability and energy conservation in low-duty-cycle WSN applications by reducing unnecessary transmissions and improving medium access efficiency [71]. 

> c: HYBRID

Hybrid protocols, such as Zebra-MAC (Z-MAC), adaptively switch between contention-based access under low traffic and TDMA-based scheduling when congestion increases, improving efficiency. More advanced approaches integrate cross-layer optimization to improve performance further. 

> d: ADAPTIVE

Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based MAC proto-cols [72] have gained attention for their ability to dynamically learn optimal transmission strategies by adapting to changing network conditions. These approaches leverage deep RL techniques to optimize channel access, minimize collisions, and improve energy efficiency without relying on predefined scheduling rules. By leveraging these alternative MAC protocols, WSNs can achieve better energy conservation, reduced latency, and increased robustness, depending on application-specific requirements. > 2) ROUTING PROTOCOLS

Routing protocols in WSNs play a crucial role in determining efficient paths for data transmission from sensor nodes to the sink while considering energy constraints, scalability, mobil-ity, and security. Selecting a suitable routing protocol depends on the network topology, communication requirements, and operational constraints. Various routing protocols have been proposed. These protocols are designed to minimize energy consumption, ensure reliability, and balance traffic loads [74]. The following paragraphs are categorized based on their key objectives and techniques. 

> a: DATA-CENTRIC

Data-centric routing protocols enhance energy efficiency in WSNs by minimizing redundant transmissions through in-network aggregation and interest-driven forwarding. Unlike traditional address-centric approaches, they employ a query-response mechanism to retrieve relevant data, dynamically adjusting transmission paths and eliminating unnecessary messages. These capabilities make data-centric protocols particularly effective for applications requiring prolonged network operation under energy constraints. One of the fundamental characteristics of data-centric routing is its ability to employ interest propagation and data aggregation to optimize communication efficiency. The sink node broadcasts an interest query to initiate data collection. Nodes that contain relevant information respond by forwarding their data along optimized paths, where intermediate nodes aggregate similar data before relaying it further. This aggregation process minimizes redundant packet transmissions, reduces congestion, and conserves energy. The total energy consumption in data-centric routing protocols can be expressed as

Directed Diffusion (DD) [77] is a well-known example that employs reinforcement-based path selection. It propagates interest messages from the sink node to establish data gra-dients, guiding packets through optimized paths. Similarly, Rumor Routing (RR) minimizes query flooding by deploying long-lived agents that traverse the network to disseminate event information. Another approach, COUGAR, introduces a query-processing layer that integrates data from multiple sources, optimizing the overall communication overhead. > III. APPLICATIONS OF WIRELESS SENSOR NETWORKS

WSNs have emerged as transformative technologies across a broad spectrum of domains, leveraging distributed sensing, real-time data processing, and adaptive communication to address complex challenges. Their applications span diverse fields such as environmental monitoring, healthcare, indus-trial automation, smart cities, precision agriculture, disaster management and emergency response, energy management and renewable energy systems, transportation and logis-tics, aquatic and underwater monitoring, space exploration and planetary research, UAVs, and military defence. This section presents a detailed examination of their applications, emphasizing scientific advancements and domain-specific methodologies. 

> A. ENVIRONMENTAL MONITORING

WSNs are fundamental to environmental monitoring due to their capability to collect high-resolution spatiotemporal data from remote and hazardous areas. They are employed for applications like microclimate monitoring, pollutant detection, and disaster prediction [128]. For instance, microclimate monitoring utilizes tempera-ture, humidity, and solar radiation sensors to model localized weather patterns. Predictive algorithms such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) analyze the temporal dynamics of these parameters, enhancing forecasting accuracy. Pollution monitoring systems deploy gas sensors to measure concen-trations of NO 2, CO 2, and particulates, refining their outputs using Bayesian estimation to address sensor inaccuracies caused by environmental drift [129], [130]. > IV. INNOVATIONS IN WSN TECHNOLOGIES

Breakthroughs in energy systems, communication protocols, data processing frameworks, and integration with emerging paradigms such as the IoT and AI have propelled WSNs’ evolution. > A. ENERGY HARVESTING AND AUTONOMOUS POWER MANAGEMENT

Energy availability is a defining constraint for WSNs. Innovations in energy harvesting technologies have shifted the paradigm from battery dependency to autonomous power systems. Solar cells remain the most mature technology, with advancements in Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithms improving efficiency under variable light conditions. For industrial environments, piezoelectric systems harvest vibrational energy from machinery, while Thermoelectric Generators (TEGs) utilize temperature gra-dients in high-heat regions such as manufacturing plants or engines [207], [208], [209]. Complementing these harvesting methods, ultra-low-power design principles in hardware and software ensure minimal energy wastage. Dynamic power scaling, duty-cycling mechanisms, and wake-up radios are now standard for managing operational energy. For instance, wake-up radios maintain nodes in a low-power state and activate them only upon detecting relevant communication signals, reducing idle listening [210], [211].

> V. CHALLENGES IN WSN APPLICATIONS

WSNs face numerous challenges that constrain their perfor-mance, scalability, and reliability. These issues arise from the inherent resource limitations of sensor nodes, dynamic deployment environments, and the increasing complexity of modern applications. Addressing these challenges requires a scientific understanding of their root causes and the development of targeted solutions. This section provides a detailed analysis of the technical and operational barriers to WSN deployment and functionality. Many of the challenges discussed in this section have been recognized since the early development of WSNs. However, they remain critical today, hindering system scalability, energy autonomy, and long-term reliability in real-world deployments. Their persistence, despite continu-ous innovation, highlights the need for renewed focus and interdisciplinary solutions tailored to emerging application contexts. 

> A. ENERGY LIMITATIONS AND DYNAMIC POWER OPTIMIZATION

Energy availability remains the most critical challenge in WSNs, directly affecting the longevity and functionality of deployments. Despite advancements in energy harvesting systems, their performance depends on environmental condi-tions, such as light availability for solar cells or temperature gradients for TEGs. This dependency introduces variability in energy supply, complicating power management in dynamic environments [267], [268]. Dynamic power optimization techniques attempt to address these limitations by adapting node operations based on real-time energy levels and task requirements. For example, stochastic models predict energy availability in hybrid harvesting systems, allowing nodes to adjust their duty cycles and communication schedules dynamically. How-ever, implementing these techniques requires computational resources, which further strain node energy reserves. Future research must focus on lightweight algorithms that balance computational overhead with power-saving benefits [269], [270], [271]. 

> B. NETWORK SCALABILITY AND CONGESTION CONTROL

Scaling WSNs to larger deployments introduces significant challenges in maintaining efficient communication and data processing. As the number of nodes increases, the network experiences higher congestion levels, packet collisions, and delays. Hierarchical clustering and tree-based routing protocols alleviate these issues by organizing nodes into manageable sub-networks, but they often require centralized control, which creates bottlenecks near the sink [272], [273]. Advanced approaches, such as adaptive clustering, utilize ML models to optimize cluster formation dynamically based on traffic patterns and energy levels. Additionally, cross-layer optimization techniques align routing, MAC protocols, and transport layers to reduce congestion holistically. These methods, while promising, demand computational and mem-ory resources that many sensor nodes lack [274], [275], [276]. 

> C. ENVIRONMENTAL INTERFERENCE AND DEPLOYMENT RESILIENCE

WSNs often operate in environments with fluctuating conditions, such as industrial sites with electromagnetic interference or underwater systems with high signal atten-uation. Environmental factors degrade communication links and sensor accuracy, necessitating robust error correction and reconfiguration mechanisms [277], [278]. Deployment resilience relies on redundancy and self-healing algorithms that reroute traffic and redistribute tasks among operational nodes during failures. For instance, network coding techniques improve data recovery by encod-ing transmitted packets, reducing the impact of packet loss. Furthermore, autonomous deployment strategies using UAVs extend network coverage and address node placement inaccuracies, but their real-time integration with existing WSNs remains an area of active research [279], [280], [281]. 

> D. SECURITY VULNERABILITIES IN RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED NODES

WSNs’ decentralized architecture, combined with their reliance on wireless communication, makes them vulnerable to a wide array of attacks, including eavesdropping, jamming, and sinkhole attacks. Conventional security solutions, such as public-key cryptography, are often unsuitable for WSNs due to their high computational and energy costs. Emerging lightweight cryptographic algorithms, such as ChaCha20 and SPECK, offer energy-efficient alternatives for encryption and authentication in resource-constrained WSN nodes [282], [283]. Additionally, blockchain-based distributed trust mech-anisms are being explored to secure decentralized WSN deployments [284], [285]. These mechanisms typically rely

> E. APPLICATION-AWARE SECURITY AND PRIVACY CONSIDERATIONS

The application domain strongly influences security and privacy challenges in WSNs. In healthcare, where WSNs support applications such as body sensor networks and remote monitoring, the sensitivity of collected physiological data demands privacy protection beyond secure transmission alone. Unauthorized access or inference attacks on patient data can have profound ethical and legal implications, especially under regulatory frameworks like HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) and GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation). Systems must balance responsiveness with privacy-preserving features such as data anonymization, selective data disclosure, and secure user authentication, without exceeding medical sensor nodes’ energy and processing limitations [288]. Similarly, in smart homes, behavioral data captured by sensor nodes poses privacy risks such as unauthorized surveil-lance and profiling if not adequately protected. In industrial automation, WSNs face cyber-physical threats including false data injection, actuator compromise, and availability-targeted attacks, which may disrupt safety-critical systems. These domain-specific risks underscore the importance of implementing security strategies that are both resource-aware and application-context sensitive [289].

> A. ULTRA-LOW-POWER AND SELF-SUSTAINING SYSTEMS

Self-sustaining nodes will integrate multi-source energy harvesting with adaptive energy management algorithms that predict environmental energy availability and adjust operational parameters accordingly. For instance, RL-based energy schedulers can optimize duty cycles dynamically, ensuring continuous operation even in environments with fluctuating energy sources. Research into micro-energy storage systems, including solid-state microbatteries and supercapacitors, is also critical for enhancing energy storage capacity without increasing the physical footprint [312], [313], [314], [315]. 

> B. INTELLIGENT AND CONTEXT-AWARE COMMUNICATION

As WSNs are deployed in increasingly dynamic and het-erogeneous environments, communication protocols must evolve to become intelligent and context-aware. The inte-gration of ML at the protocol level will enable adaptive mechanisms that adjust transmission power, routing paths, and frequency bands based on network conditions and application demands [316], [317].

Protocols leveraging RL can optimize multi-hop communication in large-scale deployments, addressing chal-lenges such as the energy hole problem and maintaining connectivity under high node density [318], [319], [320]. 

C. COLLABORATIVE AND FEDERATED INTELLIGENCE 

The future of WSNs lies in collaborative intelligence, where sensor nodes work together to analyze and interpret data, moving beyond simple data aggregation. FL, a decentralized approach to ML, allows nodes to train models while retaining their local data collaboratively. This approach not only reduces the communication overhead but also ensures data privacy, making it suitable for sensitive applications like healthcare and defense [321], [322]. Research is needed to optimize FL algorithms for resource-constrained WSNs. Techniques such as sparsification, quanti-zation, and model compression can reduce the computational and communication costs associated with collaborative intelligence. Furthermore, integrating edge servers to act as intermediaries between nodes and cloud systems will enhance scalability and processing capabilities [323], [324], [325]. 

D. QUANTUM SENSING AND COMMUNICATION 

Quantum technologies hold significant potential for advanc-ing the capabilities of WSNs. Quantum sensors, leveraging phenomena such as quantum entanglement and superposi-tion, offer unprecedented sensitivity and accuracy in detect-ing physical parameters like magnetic fields, temperature, and gravitational waves. These sensors could transform applications in environmental monitoring, healthcare, and space exploration [326], [327], [328]. Quantum communication protocols, such as Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), promise unbreakable security by utilizing the principles of quantum mechanics to detect eavesdropping. Future WSNs could integrate quantum com-munication technologies to safeguard critical data transmis-sions, particularly in defense and infrastructure monitoring applications [329], [330].

While quantum technologies offer significant potential, their integration into WSNs remains a long-term goal. Current quantum communication systems are not yet minia-turized or energy-efficient enough to meet the stringent constraints of typical sensor nodes. Most advancements are still at the experimental stage or limited to high-end applications. Progress in integrated quantum circuits and photonics may eventually enable compact quantum modules suitable for specialized WSN deployments. 

> E. BIO-INSPIRED AND SELF-ADAPTIVE ARCHITECTURES

Bio-inspired architectures, modeled after biological systems, are emerging as a promising approach to designing resilient and efficient WSNs. Techniques such as swarm intelligence, genetic algorithms, and neural-inspired learning mechanisms allow networks to adapt dynamically to environmental changes and node failures [331], [332]. For example, swarm intelligence algorithms mimic the collective behavior of social insects to optimize routing paths and resource allocation in large-scale WSNs. Neural-inspired architectures enable nodes to process sensory inputs and adapt their operations based on local observations, improving fault tolerance and reducing energy consumption. These self-adaptive systems will play a crucial role in ensuring network longevity and robustness in unpredictable environments [333], [334]. 

> F. WSNs IN EXTREME ENVIRONMENTS

Expanding the application of WSNs to extreme environments —such as deep oceans, polar regions, and outer space— presents unique challenges that require innovative solutions. Underwater WSNs, for instance, face high latency and limited bandwidth due to acoustic communication. Research into hybrid communication methods, combining acoustic, optical, and radio frequency technologies, aims to overcome these limitations [335], [336], [337]. In space exploration, WSNs must operate autonomously under extreme radiation and temperature variations. Radiation-hardened hardware and fault-tolerant algorithms will be critical for ensuring reliability. Additionally, lightweight protocols for interplanetary communication are necessary to enable real-time data exchange between planetary sensor networks and orbital spacecraft [338], [339], [340]. 

> G. INTEGRATION WITH DIGITAL TWINS

Digital Twins, virtual replicas of physical systems, are poised to revolutionize WSN applications by enabling advanced simulations, predictive analytics, and real-time monitoring. WSNs will serve as the primary data acquisition layer for Digital Twins, continuously feeding them with real-world observations [341], [342]. Future research will focus on seamless integration between WSNs and Digital Twins, emphasizing low-latency commu-nication and data consistency. For example, in smart city management, Digital Twins could simulate the impact of policy changes on traffic flow or energy consumption using real-time data from WSNs. Ensuring synchronization and scalability in these integrated systems will be key to their success [343], [344]. 

> H. SECURITY AND PRIVACY IN EMERGING APPLICATIONS

As WSNs expand into applications involving sensitive data, such as personalized healthcare and smart infrastructure, ensuring security and privacy will become increasingly important. Future research will explore advanced cryp-tographic techniques, such as homomorphic encryption, which allows data to be processed without being decrypted, preserving privacy while enabling analytics [345], [346], [347]. Decentralized security frameworks like blockchain-based authentication and access control will also gain traction. These systems will eliminate single points of failure and enhance trust in multi-vendor deployments. Moreover, anomaly detection systems leveraging deep learning will identify security breaches in real time, reducing the response time to cyberattacks [348], [349], [350]. 

> I. MULTI-MODAL AND MULTI-SENSOR FUSION

The integration of multi-modal sensing in WSNs enables richer datasets and more comprehensive analyses. Future trends will focus on efficient fusion techniques that combine data from heterogeneous sensors, such as image, acoustic, and environmental sensors, to improve decision-making accuracy [351], [352]. For instance, in precision agriculture, data from soil moisture sensors, drones, and weather stations can be combined using fusion algorithms to optimize irrigation and pest control. In healthcare, integrating physiological signals like ECG, SpO 2, and motion data will enhance diagnostic precision. Research into lightweight and real-time fusion algorithms will be crucial for extending these capabilities to resource-constrained WSNs [353], [354], [355]. VII. CONCLUSION 

WSNs have emerged as a cornerstone of modern technology, addressing critical challenges across diverse domains such as environmental monitoring, healthcare, industrial automation, and beyond. The advancements in energy harvesting, commu-nication protocols, and data processing have enabled WSNs to transcend traditional limitations, offering scalable, reliable, and efficient solutions. However, the ever-expanding scope of WSN applications brings with it complex challenges and emerging research gaps that demand innovative approaches. One of the central themes in the evolution of WSNs is achieving sustainability through energy efficiency and self-sustaining systems. Innovations such as multi-source energy harvesting and dynamic power management algorithms represent significant strides toward prolonging network lifespans, particularly in remote and resource-constrained environments. These developments ensure that WSNs can maintain functionality in diverse settings, from dense urban areas to extreme environments. Integrating WSNs with emerging paradigms such as IoT, AI, and digital twins highlights their pivotal role in shaping future technologies. Adopting intelligent protocols and collaborative processing frameworks has transformed WSNs into data collection networks and platforms for real-time analytics and autonomous decision-making. FL and edge intelligence exemplify the potential for distributed processing, ensuring that WSNs remain viable even in

Scalability issues in dense networks, dynamic topology management, and robust security are persistent obstacles that must be addressed through cutting-edge research. Developing lightweight cryptographic methods and blockchain-based trust mechanisms is essential for safeguarding sensitive data in applications such as healthcare, defense, and industrial automation. Similarly, quantum communication and bio-inspired architectures are set to redefine the boundaries of what WSNs can achieve regarding reliability and adaptability. This study contributes a concise review of the current landscape of WSNs, structured around three dimensions: (i) domain-specific applications, (ii) technological innovations such as energy-aware and AI-integrated systems, and (iii) challenge-driven analysis across areas including energy effi-ciency, scalability, and security. Furthermore, comparative and case-based tabular summaries are presented to bridge theoretical advancements with real-world implementations. Future research should prioritize the development of hybrid energy harvesting models with adaptive power scheduling, lightweight and context-sensitive security proto-cols, and resilient WSN frameworks capable of autonomous reconfiguration in extreme environments such as underwater, polar, and space missions. In parallel, optimized 5G-enabled architectures, fog-assisted intelligence, and seamless interoperability must be advanced to enhance real-time data processing and reduce latency. Cross-domain integration with Digital Twins, FL, and self-organizing systems will be critical to realizing the full potential of next-generation WSNs. The trajectory of WSN development underscores their potential as transformative enablers across scientific, indus-trial, and societal domains. By addressing these open challenges and embracing interdisciplinary collaboration, WSNs are poised to become integral to the next wave of technological innovation across both Earth-bound and remote environments.
