###### Qualifications

I am a highly accomplished academic professional. I have been involved in several IEEE activities during the last years, and I believe that the acquired experience enables me to apply for this prestigious position in VTS. My past roles in VTS show how committed I am to the activities I am involved in. For instance, I have learnt a lot as Associate Editor of IEEE TVT since 2012, position in which I was awarded several times in recognition to the excellent service. I have also been Track Chair in previous IEEE VTCs editions and Technical Program Chair of IEEE VTC2021/2022-Spring, and the email exchanges and interactions with authors, track chairs, and members of the organizing committee enriched considerably my body of knowledge. I also led the creation of two VTS Chapters in South America. In 2019, Brazilian VTS Chapter was awarded the Chapter of the Year. I was Vice-Chair of the VTS Propagation Committee from 2023 to 2025, and I am Editor-in-Chief of the IEEE Communications Letters since July 1st, 2023. However, I understand that I have much more to contribute, and this is the reason I am applying for the BoG of VTS. I think that my candidacy can serve as a bridge for expanding the VTS activities throughout Latin America and Middle East, in addition to keeping the geographical diversity among the BoG members. I am highly motivated and will be fully committed to the new role (if elected).

###### Major Accomplishments

*   Certificate of Appreciation of Top Associate Editor for outstanding contributions to IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology in 2013, 2015, and 2016.

*   As the Latin-American Chapter Coordinator of the VTS, I was responsible for the creation of the Brazilian VTS Chapter and Colombia VTS Chapter in South America. In 2019, the recently created Brazilian VTS Chapter was awarded as the Chapter of the Year.

*   Top 1% Scientists in the World – broad field of Electronics and Electrical Engineering (source: Research.com).

**Statement:**If elected to be part of the Board of Governors of VTS, I intend to work hard with all members to consolidate VTS as one of the world’s most relevant societies for vehicular technologies and communications. I’ll make hard efforts to increase the VTS internationalization, particularly towards developing countries, such as Brazil, and towards the Middle East region, where I am currently living. I also plan to discuss and develop new ways to attract and involve new members in the society.

During his work at BMW, he worked on causal machine learning; neuromorphic and quantum computing; big data and machine learning for improving driving behavior and enabling intelligent driving; and applying AI to improve vehicle diagnostics, manufacturing and BMW’s internal processes. Dr. Chin has authored more than 30 publications and 10 patents, including pending. He received a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Toronto, MASc in Computer Engineering from the University of Waterloo and BASc from the University of Waterloo. He has previously worked for Nokia Research Center, Nokia and Microsoft in Beijing, China. Dr. Chin is active in the community in data science and machine learning meetups, as member of various program committees of academic conferences, and has given more than 50 talks to universities, meetups and conferences.

###### Qualifications

What makes me an ideal candidate for this position is that I have been active in the IEEE Vehicular Technology Society Chicago Chapter for 7 years as Chair where I organize chapter meetings with speakers in the vehicular technology industry. I have also been active in the IEEE Vehicular Technology Conference since 2017, serving in various conference leadership roles as Panelist in 2017, Program Committee member in 2018 Spring conference, Industry Sessions Co-Chair and Industry Panel Chair for Connected and Autonomous Driving in 2018 Fall conference, Industry Sessions Co-chair and Keynote Chair for Connected and Autonomous Driving in 2019 Fall conference, and Publicity Co-chair in 2020 Fall conference. For the past 4 years, I have been appointed as Chair of the IEEE VTS Industry Engagement Committee to help promote industry to participate in the IEEE Vehicular Technology Conference and IEEE Vehicular Technology Society. As shown from above, I have been Chair of other IEEE conference committees besides VTC. I also have leadership experience in board committees such as The Mid-America Club and The Metropolitan Club (a private business and social club) and my own condominium board association. I was the Chair of the IEEE Chicago Section (2023-2024), and I am currently the Chair of the IEEE Computer Society Chicago Chapter and Secretary of the IEEE Connected and Autonomous Vehicles Standards Committee. My passion for engaging the Chicago community in IEEE Chicago from the IEEE Chicago 125th Anniversary Event as Publicity Chair in 2019, led to me becoming Chair for the IEEE Chicago 126th Anniversary Event held in 2020 and Chair for the IEEE Chicago 129th Anniversary held in 2023. Therefore, all these leadership positions described above show my dedicated leadership qualities, which I believe will serve me well as a Member of the VTS Board of Governors.

###### Major Accomplishments

One major contribution that I brought to the IEEE Vehicular Technology Conference 2018-Fall in Chicago, is that I advocated for a Panel on Connected and Autonomous Vehicles to show the topics that needed to be addressed in this area, which was not addressed in previous conferences. I took charge of this Panel and I convinced my company, BMW, to be a sponsor of the conference. I saw there were few automotive companies in this conference since the conference was more of an academic nature. I also was a member of the conference committee and contributed my thoughts on how to attract more industry professionals to attend this conference, which included providing a discounted one-day pass to industry professionals. Second, I was looking to join the IEEE Vehicular Technology Society Chicago Chapter, but discovered that this chapter had dissolved due to a lack of leadership. I volunteered to become the Chair of this chapter. The chapter was revived 6 years ago and has been successful with at least 4 meetings per year, along with being able to get successful funding from the IEEE VTS Chapters Chair. Third, while I was working for Nokia Research Center, I contributed to creating a new team and research area for Mobile Social Networking. I suggested this research area by writing a technical report and proposal which was read by the Director of the Nokia Research Center lab in Beijing. The Director decided to create the Mobile Social Networking Team and made me the Project Lead for a mobile social networking project which became Nokia Find & Connect, an application used for conferences and meetings for connecting with people. This contributed to Nokia with the publication of 1 patent and 10 research papers.

**Statement:**If I am selected for this position, I would like to have a plan to involve more professionals from the automotive industry, vehicular technology and transportation industries to join the IEEE Vehicular Technology Society. This would be achieved by providing industry professionals a discounted IEEE VTS membership and have them be involved in IEEE VTS standards activities as well as involvement in the IEEE VTS conferences. As well, companies in the industry would have the opportunity at a conference discount, to be a sponsor or have a booth showcasing their products as well as being able to provide recruiting activities to the many students who are looking for career opportunities during these conferences. I would also propose having a separate industry track in the IEEE VTC conferences to allow industry researchers and industry professionals to submit papers in this area. Often, they would not submit before because the tracks were more of an academic and theoretical nature. I want to dramatically expand industry engagement in VTS. I have the experience and commitment to achieve this goal.

I currently serve as Senior Editor for IEEE Vehicular Technology Magazine and have been Guest Editor for leading VTS publications. As Canada Research Chair in Efficient Electric Vehicles, I lead the e-TESC Lab and have authored over 245 publications.

###### Major Accomplishments

Within IEEE VTS, I’ve had the opportunity to contribute meaningfully by helping organize the first two joint editions of VPPC and VTC-Fall, in 2018 and again in 2024. As General Chair of VPPC in 2018, I led the first-ever co-location of these two flagship conferences. This initiative brought together the transportation and wireless communication communities, encouraging stronger collaboration and attracting broad participation. My continued involvement in the 2024 edition helped build on this momentum, reinforcing the interdisciplinary links between the Society’s core areas and supporting VTS’s strategic development.

On the professional side, one of my most significant contributions has been the creation and leadership of the electric-Transport, Energy Storage and Conversion (e-TESC) Laboratory at the University of Sherbrooke, where I hold the Canada Research Chair in Efficient Electric Vehicles with Hybridized Energy Storage Systems. Since founding the lab, I’ve led a multidisciplinary team that includes 3 faculty members, 2 postdoctoral researchers, 8 PhD students, and 2 research assistants. Our work—fully funded through external grants—focuses on electric mobility, hybrid energy storage, energy management, and next-generation powertrains. The lab is known for its applied, collaborative approach and strong ties with both industry and academia.

To date, I’ve authored or co-authored more than 245 peer-reviewed publications and lead several national and international research projects in close partnership with academic institutions, companies, and public agencies.

**Statement:** I believe the IEEE Vehicular Technology Society plays a central role in advancing innovation and facilitating knowledge exchange in wireless communications, land transportation, and motor vehicles—the three pillars that define its technical scope. As these areas evolve rapidly, particularly with the growing importance of electric mobility, energy systems, and intelligent transportation, VTS must remain a leading platform for collaboration and forward-looking research.

If elected to the Board of Governors, I will work to strengthen the Society’s global presence by enhancing the quality and visibility of our conferences, journals, and standards initiatives. Ensuring our technical activities remain relevant, inclusive, and aligned with emerging challenges is essential to maintaining VTS’s leadership.

Supporting young professionals and early-career researchers is a key part of my vision. I will promote mentorship, networking, and development opportunities to help them grow and engage with the Society. These efforts are vital to cultivating the next generation of contributors and leaders.

Having served as General Chair and TPC Chair for flagship VTS events, Senior Editor of Vehicular Technology Magazine, and in other editorial and organizational roles, I bring experience and strong commitment. I look forward to continuing to serve VTS and contributing to its strategic growth and impact.

# Investigation of a Method for Identifying Sensor Information Using a Constrained Database Update Algorithm in Physical Wireless Parameter Conversion Sensor Networks

ABSTRACT Large-scale wireless sensor networks (WSNs) comprising multiple sensors accessing the network simultaneously have gained considerable attention owing to the proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT). However, the increasing collision rates and header redundancy in packet-oriented WSNs severely degrade the transmission efficiency. In this study, we proposed a wide-area environmental recognition scheme that identifies the source sensors in Physical Wireless Parameter Conversion Sensor Networks (PhyC-SN), which features headerless transmissions without embedding sensor IDs, by integrating it with a Mobile Data Gathering Station (MDGS). The scheme controls the number of simultaneous accesses and cross-references the candidate sensors and observed channels across multiple aggregation points to localize the source sensor of each reported value. To prevent breakdowns in the sensor information correspondence caused by the missing data and misestimated sensor counts arising from the upper bound of the sensor count identification of PhyC-SN, we further designed constraint-aware database updating algorithms: the Integrity Verification Algorithm (IVA) and enhanced IVA (EIVA). In a real wireless environment, the proposed EIVA attained an identification rate exceeding 0.95 at a request-signal threshold of −90 dBm. In large-scale simulations under a fixed threshold of −100 dBm, EIVA achieved a median identification rate of approximately 1.0, outperforming the baseline algorithms. These results indicate that controlling the aggregation range via the request-signal threshold, combined with the constraint-aware staged updates, enables high-accuracy source-sensor identification even under missing data and misestimation.

In conventional WSNs, packet-based communication is the dominant paradigm in which each sensor converts its measurement into a packet and sequentially transmits it to a base station [4], [5]. However, as the number of sensors increases, simultaneous channel access causes frequent packet collisions and retransmissions, which significantly degrades the packet arrival rate [6], [7]. Moreover, the address fields must be lengthened as the device population increases; when the payload is small (e.g., in typical sensor readings), the header overhead per packet becomes dominant and severely reduces the transmission efficiency [8]. In this study, we proposed a novel communication framework called Physical Wireless Parameter Conversion Sensor Networks (PhyC-SN) [9] to address these issues. In PhyC-SN, each sensor selects a unique frequency channel corresponding to its measured physical quantity and transmits an unmodulated carrier. Subsequently, the receiver infers the transmitted information from the index of the frequency channel in which the carrier is observed. Multiple sensors concurrently transmit carriers at frequencies mapped to their information values; thus, the received signal forms a frequency spectrum in which carriers are superposed across channels. The receiver can count the number of sensors that transmitted simultaneously by analyzing the characteristic features of this spectrum. Consequently, the system instanta-neously obtains the statistical tendency of the reported sensor information (e.g., frequency histograms) over all the sensors accessing the medium. PhyC-SN presents three major advantages. First, the protocol overhead is minimal as the sensors transmit carriers without headers. Second, a complex medium-access control is unnecessary and reduces the probability of information loss. Third, when compared with per-sensor reporting, PhyC-SN reduces the aggregation latency and helps in instantaneously estimating the statistical tendency over all the accessing sensors. These properties make PhyC-SN well-suited for wireless environments, where a large number of sensors compete for access in large-scale sensor networks. In PhyC-SN, multiple sensors may report the same information value. When carriers are transmitted over the same channel, the received power ideally scales with the number of sensors accessing the network. This behavior can be exploited to determine the number of sensors that have reported the same value. However, under multipath fading, carriers may add noncoherently, inducing large fluctuations in the received power and severely degrading the accuracy of sensor-count identification [10]. We established a method that augments the received power with the statistical trends of the sensor-specific frequency jitter and channel responses to identify the sensor count to overcome this challenge [11]. This method leverages features beyond the received power alone to realize robust sensor-count identification even in multipath environments. However, this approach faces an upper bound on the identifiable sensor count. When the true number exceeds this bound, the count is underestimated, thereby causing identification errors. Additionally, PhyC-SN aggregates statistics without attaching sensor IDs. Therefore, constructing heat maps depicting spatial conditions based on the region is challenging, which limits monitoring tasks that rely on such maps. Therefore, we proposed integrating PhyC-SN with aMobile Data Gathering Station (MDGS) to collect the environmental information over a specific region [12]. MDGS employs drones or vehicles as mobile collectors that visit multiple waypoints to obtain the sensor information. By constraining the access range between the sensors and MDGS, the number of simultaneous accesses can be reduced, thereby enabling stable statistical estimates under PhyC-SN. In the proposed framework, the MDGS periodically broad-casts a request signal and sensors that receive the request respond by transmitting carriers at the frequencies mapped by PhyC-SN to their information values, which are then received by the MDGS. Each sensor determines whether to transmit based on the received power of the request signal. This limits the set of responding sensors and prevents information loss, even when a sensor-count identifier with an upper bound is used [11]. Furthermore, MDGS associates its position with each PhyC-SN aggregation by repeating the movement and aggregation. A specific sensor may respond to requests received from different MDGS positions as the MDGS moves around it; thus, the same information value is observed at multiple MDGS locations. The source sensor that generated the information could be localized based on the spatial pattern of the MDGS reception positions, thereby enabling the construction of a heat map. Increasing the request-signal transmission power in MDGS-based aggregation enables the collection of infor-mation from a wider area. For a fixed monitoring region, increasing the aggregation width reduces the total travel distance required for the MDGS to cover all the sen-sors, thereby reducing the collection time and number of aggregation cycles. However, this increases the number of simultaneous accesses and may exceed the identifiable upper bound, thereby causing information loss. Therefore, the request-signal power must be designed to maximize the spatial coverage while avoiding information loss, thereby minimizing the aggregation time and cycles. Moreover, the proposed method localizes the source sensors from the combinations of the MDGS positions and the observed sensor-count patterns. If the sensor count is misidentified, an incorrect MDGS pattern may be registered, causing erroneous source localization. Hence, a source localization algorithm that is robust against MDGS-pattern misestimation must be developed. In this study, we considered mobile aggregation via MDGS and proposed an algorithm that establishes correspondence between the sensors and information values based on mul-tiple PhyC-SN aggregation results. The proposed algorithm lists the information values aggregated at multiple MDGS

> II. RELATED WORKS

The number of sensors has increased drastically owing to the proliferation of IoT. Consequently, data collection in large-scale WSNs typically experiences packet access beyond the admissible device population, causing severe degradation in the packet arrival rates [13]. In conventional WSNs and in various wireless systems, packet transmission is assumed, and extensive studies were conducted on the MAC layer to ensure stable access through collision avoidance and retransmission control. For example, TDMA-based dynamic slot assignment was proposed to avoid collisions [14]. Other studies have also leveraged compressed sensing to avoid packet collisions while achieving large-scale energy-efficient data collection [15]. Additionally, interference suppression techniques have been analyzed to improve the packet arrival rates and to miti-gate the packet collisions caused by simultaneous access. The representative approaches include successive interference cancellation (SIC) [16], parallel interference cancellation (PIC) [17], and maximum likelihood (ML) detection [18], machine-learning-based methods [19], methods based on compressed sensing [20], and collision-resolving techniques tailored to low-power wide-area networks (LPWANs) that exploit LPWAN-specific signal waveforms [21]. These approaches depend on the fact that wireless propagation imprints device-specific characteristics, such as the ampli-tude, phase, coding, and transmit timing, on the transmitted signals, thereby enabling signal separation. However, these features must be increasingly fine-grained owing to the increase in the device population, presenting concerns regarding the received power required to maintain an increase in the identification accuracy. Moreover, the header bits required to identify the individual packets scale with the number of devices, thereby considerably increasing the protocol overhead. While recent deep-learning-based approaches have sub-stantially extended these classical techniques—for example, model-based deep receivers [22], low-complexity deep MIMO detectors [23], and sequential deep models for NOMA multiuser detection [24]—they still rely on pilot sequences or known signatures for device identification, preserving the fundamental dependence on header-based signaling. Conversely, the PhyC-SN framework [9] does not attach header information for device identification. Therefore, its overhead is inherently less susceptible to growth with the device population. Additionally, the probability that an excessively large number of devices will simultaneously access the same frequency is low as the access signal is a narrowband. Even when multiple devices access the same channel, the number of accessing nodes can be determined by exploiting the fluctuations [10] in the received power and device-specific frequency jitter [11]. Consequently, PhyC-SN presents the advantages of low redundancy and stable information aggregation, even in large-scale sensor networks, where several sensors compete for access. For large-scale WSNs, several studies have analyzed the use of mobile platforms—such as drones and autonomous ground robots, as base stations to address the increase in transmission power associated with long-range communica-tion [25]. These studies deployed multiple uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) or mobile sinks and employed clustering and tour optimization strategies to achieve energy efficiency and spatially distribute the sensor access for efficient data

gathering [26], [27]. Other works emphasized collision-free scheduling by jointly planning the mobile station placement/ trajectories and transmission control to avoid packet colli-sions [28]. In another study, the UAV was considered as a cluster head and packet collisions were reduced via local aggregation [29]. From a different perspective, UAVs have also been employed as intermediate relays to forward sensor data from ground devices to base stations, rather than directly gathering data themselves [30]. Recent studies have extended these static clustering- and tour-based approaches toward frameworks that adapt to more dynamic and long-term operational settings. Representative directions include joint sensing scheduling and trajectory optimization for multi-UAV systems under AoI (Age of Information) constraints [31], deep-reinforcement-learning-based adaptive UAV trajectory planning [32], and integrated charging scheduling and trajectory design for persistent data collection under UAV battery constraints [33], indicating a shift from single-mission tour optimization toward long-term operational frameworks. In all such approaches, moving the collector reduces the communication distance to the sensors, thereby presenting benefits such as reduced power consumption and collision avoidance using fewer simultaneously accessing devices. When the physically aggregable range is limited, only the sensors within that range can be reported, thereby inducing a correspondence between the position of the collector and the set of reportable sensors. This correspondence can be exploited to identify the source sensor for a reported item. Hence, even in PhyC-SN, where explicit sensor IDs are not attached, the source sensors can be localized, thereby enabling the construction of heat maps annotated with information sources, which is difficult to achieve using only PhyC-SN. Thus, leveraging the MDGS position information to identify the source sensors of the transmitted information in an ID-reduced PhyC-SN is a challenging and, to the best of our knowledge, novel research direction. Unlike the packet-based MAC, interference-cancellation, and deep-learning approaches discussed above, which dis-tinguish devices from features embedded in or carried by the transmitted signal, the proposed framework requires no such per-device signaling. Moreover, whereas existing mobile-platform studies exploit collector mobility mainly for energy efficiency and collision avoidance, the present work uses the collector’s position information itself as the basis for source-sensor identification. 

> III. SYSTEM OVERVIEW

This paper proposes a framework for wide-area envi-ronmental recognition using Physical Wireless Parameter Conversion Sensor Networks (PhyC-SN) that identifies the correspondence between observed sensor information and source sensors without attaching sensor IDs. Fig. 1 illustrates the overview of the proposed method. In PhyC-SN, each sensor converts its physical measurement (e.g., temperature) into a frequency channel and transmits a headerless carrier signal (Fig. 1(a)). At the receiver, a spectrum representing the superposition of signals from multiple sensors is observed. While this approach reduces protocol overhead, multiple sensors may select the same channel, making it difficult to directly identify which sensor transmitted which information. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a Mobile Data Gathering Station (MDGS) (Fig. 1(b)). The MDGS traverses multiple aggregation points, broadcasts a request signal at each point, and collects PhyC-SN responses from sensors within its coverage. At each aggregation point, the system records the candidate sensors that could have responded and the channels that were actually observed (Fig. 1(c)). The key idea of the proposed method is to identify the correspondence between individual sensors and their channels by cross-referencing records from multiple aggre-gation points (Fig. 1(d)). For example, if a sensor could respond at both Point 1 and Point 2, and only one channel is commonly observed at both points, then that sensor’s transmitted channel can be uniquely identified. This paper designs a database update algorithm that performs such cross-referencing efficiently and robustly, achieving high-accuracy sensor information identification even in the presence of missing data and estimation errors. The details of PhyC-SN are described in Section IV, the observation procedure and record format using MDGS in Section V, and the proposed algorithm in Section VI.

V. WIDE-AREA ENVIRONMENTAL RECOGNITION USING A MOBILE DATA GATHERING STATION 

A. OVERVIEW OF MDGS 

Figure 4 depicts the concept by which an MDGS obtains the PhyC-SN frequency distributions at multiple aggregation points. The MDGS broadcasts a request signal, and the sensors respond by transmitting an unmodulated carrier at a frequency corresponding to their observed (quantized) infor-mation. Each sensor accumulates the energy of the received request signal and responds only when the accumulated energy exceeds a specific threshold, Rth , which mitigates power fluctuations caused by multipath fading. The MDGS effectively restricts the responding sensors to those within a certain distance by comparing the accumulated request signal energy with the threshold. A higher Rth causes the responses to be obtained primarily from the sensors closer to the MDGS. In this study, for each aggregation point, k, of the MDGS (k = 1, 2, . . . ) and a given threshold, Rth , we assume that a set of sensors capable of receiving the request, Sk,Rth ⊆ S

(where S denotes the set of all sensors), was established a priori. In particular, at the time of sensor deployment, each sensor determines whether the request signal is receivable at the candidate aggregation points of the MDGS; based on this, we prepared the following prior information to establish the sensor sets.

VIII. CONCLUSION 

In this study, we proposed the EIVA, a constraint-aware sensor-information identification algorithm for wide-area environmental recognition that integrates PhyC-SN with an MDGS. EIVA explicitly accounts for the missing labels and misestimation attributed to exceeding the sensor count iden-tification upper bound Nth . By updating only those channels that can be certified to satisfy the upper bound condition and by deferring and re-evaluating uncertain decisions via staged updates, EIVA suppresses the accumulation of incorrect correspondences. The evaluation demonstrated that: (i) for MDGS ×PhyC-SN aggregation using real measurement data, EIVA effec-tively identified sensor information even under missing labels and recognition errors, and (ii) in large-scale WSN simulations, EIVA achieved a higher identification rate and lower MAE than the conventional methods under high density and high-missing conditions. Consequently, highly reliable environmental recognition was enabled while retaining the advantages of PhyC-SN, thereby reducing the packet headers, simplifying access control, and mitigating the impact of collisions causing missing information. Regarding practical considerations, synchronization among sensors is handled within the cyclic prefix duration. The selection of Nth = 3 is supported by our experimental results, which show that this value balances classification accuracy and label saturation. The threshold Rth controls the trade-off between spatial coverage and identification reliability. In summary, integrating localized aggregation using MDGS with EIVA constraint-aware staged updates man-ages the risks of missing information and misassignment caused by exceeding Nth , thereby enabling high-accuracy sensor-information identification via progressive database updates.

TOSHI ITO  1, OSAMU TAKYU  1, (Member, IEEE), MAI OHTA 2, (Member, IEEE), TAKEO FUJII  3, (Senior Member, IEEE), AND KOICHI ADACHI  4, (Senior Member, IEEE)

Corresponding author: Toshi Ito (24hs202a@shinshu-u.ac.jp) This work was supported in part by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, Japan, through the Strategic Information and Communications Research and Development Promotion Programme (SCOPE) under Grant JP235004002; and in part by the Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST) Support for Pioneering Research Initiated by the Next Generation (SPRING), Japan, Shinshu University under Grant JPMJSP2144. 

ABSTRACT Large-scale wireless sensor networks (WSNs) comprising multiple sensors accessing the network simultaneously have gained considerable attention owing to the proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT). However, the increasing collision rates and header redundancy in packet-oriented WSNs severely degrade the transmission efficiency. In this study, we proposed a wide-area environmental recognition scheme that identifies the source sensors in Physical Wireless Parameter Conversion Sensor Networks (PhyC-SN), which features headerless transmissions without embedding sensor IDs, by integrating it with a Mobile Data Gathering Station (MDGS). The scheme controls the number of simultaneous accesses and cross-references the candidate sensors and observed channels across multiple aggregation points to localize the source sensor of each reported value. To prevent breakdowns in the sensor information correspondence caused by the missing data and misestimated sensor counts arising from the upper bound of the sensor count identification of PhyC-SN, we further designed constraint-aware database updating algorithms: the Integrity Verification Algorithm (IVA) and enhanced IVA (EIVA). In a real wireless environment, the proposed EIVA attained an identification rate exceeding 0.95 at a request-signal threshold of −90 dBm. In large-scale simulations under a fixed threshold of −100 dBm, EIVA achieved a median identification rate of approximately 1.0, outperforming the baseline algorithms. These results indicate that controlling the aggregation range via the request-signal threshold, combined with the constraint-aware staged updates, enables high-accuracy source-sensor identification even under missing data and misestimation.

I. INTRODUCTION 

Sensor networks are being increasingly employed for disaster monitoring, agricultural management, and urban

In conventional WSNs, packet-based communication is the dominant paradigm in which each sensor converts its measurement into a packet and sequentially transmits it to a base station [4], [5]. However, as the number of sensors increases, simultaneous channel access causes frequent packet collisions and retransmissions, which significantly degrades the packet arrival rate [6], [7]. Moreover, the address fields must be lengthened as the device population increases; when the payload is small (e.g., in typical sensor readings), the header overhead per packet becomes dominant and severely reduces the transmission efficiency [8]. In this study, we proposed a novel communication framework called Physical Wireless Parameter Conversion Sensor Networks (PhyC-SN) [9] to address these issues. In PhyC-SN, each sensor selects a unique frequency channel corresponding to its measured physical quantity and transmits an unmodulated carrier. Subsequently, the receiver infers the transmitted information from the index of the frequency channel in which the carrier is observed. Multiple sensors concurrently transmit carriers at frequencies mapped to their information values; thus, the received signal forms a frequency spectrum in which carriers are superposed across channels. The receiver can count the number of sensors that transmitted simultaneously by analyzing the characteristic features of this spectrum. Consequently, the system instanta-neously obtains the statistical tendency of the reported sensor information (e.g., frequency histograms) over all the sensors accessing the medium. PhyC-SN presents three major advantages. First, the protocol overhead is minimal as the sensors transmit carriers without headers. Second, a complex medium-access control is unnecessary and reduces the probability of information loss. Third, when compared with per-sensor reporting, PhyC-SN reduces the aggregation latency and helps in instantaneously estimating the statistical tendency over all the accessing sensors. These properties make PhyC-SN well-suited for wireless environments, where a large number of sensors compete for access in large-scale sensor networks. In PhyC-SN, multiple sensors may report the same information value. When carriers are transmitted over the same channel, the received power ideally scales with the number of sensors accessing the network. This behavior can be exploited to determine the number of sensors that have reported the same value. However, under multipath fading, carriers may add noncoherently, inducing large fluctuations in the received power and severely degrading the accuracy of sensor-count identification [10]. We established a method that augments the received power with the statistical trends of the sensor-specific frequency jitter and channel responses to identify the sensor count to overcome this challenge [11]. This method leverages features beyond the received power alone to realize robust sensor-count identification even in multipath environments. However, this approach faces an upper bound on the identifiable sensor count. When the true number exceeds this bound, the count is underestimated, thereby causing identification errors. Additionally, PhyC-SN aggregates statistics without attaching sensor IDs. Therefore, constructing heat maps depicting spatial conditions based on the region is challenging, which limits monitoring tasks that rely on such maps. Therefore, we proposed integrating PhyC-SN with aMobile Data Gathering Station (MDGS) to collect the environmental information over a specific region [12]. MDGS employs drones or vehicles as mobile collectors that visit multiple waypoints to obtain the sensor information. By constraining the access range between the sensors and MDGS, the number of simultaneous accesses can be reduced, thereby enabling stable statistical estimates under PhyC-SN. In the proposed framework, the MDGS periodically broad-casts a request signal and sensors that receive the request respond by transmitting carriers at the frequencies mapped by PhyC-SN to their information values, which are then received by the MDGS. Each sensor determines whether to transmit based on the received power of the request signal. This limits the set of responding sensors and prevents information loss, even when a sensor-count identifier with an upper bound is used [11]. Furthermore, MDGS associates its position with each PhyC-SN aggregation by repeating the movement and aggregation. A specific sensor may respond to requests received from different MDGS positions as the MDGS moves around it; thus, the same information value is observed at multiple MDGS locations. The source sensor that generated the information could be localized based on the spatial pattern of the MDGS reception positions, thereby enabling the construction of a heat map. Increasing the request-signal transmission power in MDGS-based aggregation enables the collection of infor-mation from a wider area. For a fixed monitoring region, increasing the aggregation width reduces the total travel distance required for the MDGS to cover all the sen-sors, thereby reducing the collection time and number of aggregation cycles. However, this increases the number of simultaneous accesses and may exceed the identifiable upper bound, thereby causing information loss. Therefore, the request-signal power must be designed to maximize the spatial coverage while avoiding information loss, thereby minimizing the aggregation time and cycles. Moreover, the proposed method localizes the source sensors from the combinations of the MDGS positions and the observed sensor-count patterns. If the sensor count is misidentified, an incorrect MDGS pattern may be registered, causing erroneous source localization. Hence, a source localization algorithm that is robust against MDGS-pattern misestimation must be developed. In this study, we considered mobile aggregation via MDGS and proposed an algorithm that establishes correspondence between the sensors and information values based on mul-tiple PhyC-SN aggregation results. The proposed algorithm lists the information values aggregated at multiple MDGS

> II. RELATED WORKS

The number of sensors has increased drastically owing to the proliferation of IoT. Consequently, data collection in large-scale WSNs typically experiences packet access beyond the admissible device population, causing severe degradation in the packet arrival rates [13]. In conventional WSNs and in various wireless systems, packet transmission is assumed, and extensive studies were conducted on the MAC layer to ensure stable access through collision avoidance and retransmission control. For example, TDMA-based dynamic slot assignment was proposed to avoid collisions [14]. Other studies have also leveraged compressed sensing to avoid packet collisions while achieving large-scale energy-efficient data collection [15]. Additionally, interference suppression techniques have been analyzed to improve the packet arrival rates and to miti-gate the packet collisions caused by simultaneous access. The representative approaches include successive interference cancellation (SIC) [16], parallel interference cancellation (PIC) [17], and maximum likelihood (ML) detection [18], machine-learning-based methods [19], methods based on compressed sensing [20], and collision-resolving techniques tailored to low-power wide-area networks (LPWANs) that exploit LPWAN-specific signal waveforms [21]. These approaches depend on the fact that wireless propagation imprints device-specific characteristics, such as the ampli-tude, phase, coding, and transmit timing, on the transmitted signals, thereby enabling signal separation. However, these features must be increasingly fine-grained owing to the increase in the device population, presenting concerns regarding the received power required to maintain an increase in the identification accuracy. Moreover, the header bits required to identify the individual packets scale with the number of devices, thereby considerably increasing the protocol overhead. While recent deep-learning-based approaches have sub-stantially extended these classical techniques—for example, model-based deep receivers [22], low-complexity deep MIMO detectors [23], and sequential deep models for NOMA multiuser detection [24]—they still rely on pilot sequences or known signatures for device identification, preserving the fundamental dependence on header-based signaling. Conversely, the PhyC-SN framework [9] does not attach header information for device identification. Therefore, its overhead is inherently less susceptible to growth with the device population. Additionally, the probability that an excessively large number of devices will simultaneously access the same frequency is low as the access signal is a narrowband. Even when multiple devices access the same channel, the number of accessing nodes can be determined by exploiting the fluctuations [10] in the received power and device-specific frequency jitter [11]. Consequently, PhyC-SN presents the advantages of low redundancy and stable information aggregation, even in large-scale sensor networks, where several sensors compete for access. For large-scale WSNs, several studies have analyzed the use of mobile platforms—such as drones and autonomous ground robots, as base stations to address the increase in transmission power associated with long-range communica-tion [25]. These studies deployed multiple uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) or mobile sinks and employed clustering and tour optimization strategies to achieve energy efficiency and spatially distribute the sensor access for efficient data

From a different perspective, UAVs have also been employed as intermediate relays to forward sensor data from ground devices to base stations, rather than directly gathering data themselves [30]. Recent studies have extended these static clustering- and tour-based approaches toward frameworks that adapt to more dynamic and long-term operational settings. Representative directions include joint sensing scheduling and trajectory optimization for multi-UAV systems under AoI (Age of Information) constraints [31], deep-reinforcement-learning-based adaptive UAV trajectory planning [32], and integrated charging scheduling and trajectory design for persistent data collection under UAV battery constraints [33], indicating a shift from single-mission tour optimization toward long-term operational frameworks. In all such approaches, moving the collector reduces the communication distance to the sensors, thereby presenting benefits such as reduced power consumption and collision avoidance using fewer simultaneously accessing devices. When the physically aggregable range is limited, only the sensors within that range can be reported, thereby inducing a correspondence between the position of the collector and the set of reportable sensors. This correspondence can be exploited to identify the source sensor for a reported item. Unlike the packet-based MAC, interference-cancellation, and deep-learning approaches discussed above, which dis-tinguish devices from features embedded in or carried by the transmitted signal, the proposed framework requires no such per-device signaling. Moreover, whereas existing mobile-platform studies exploit collector mobility mainly for energy efficiency and collision avoidance, the present work uses the collector’s position information itself as the basis for source-sensor identification. 

> III. SYSTEM OVERVIEW

This paper proposes a framework for wide-area envi-ronmental recognition using Physical Wireless Parameter Conversion Sensor Networks (PhyC-SN) that identifies the correspondence between observed sensor information and source sensors without attaching sensor IDs. Fig. 1 illustrates the overview of the proposed method. In PhyC-SN, each sensor converts its physical measurement (e.g., temperature) into a frequency channel and transmits a headerless carrier signal (Fig. 1(a)). At the receiver, a spectrum representing the superposition of signals from multiple sensors is observed. While this approach reduces protocol overhead, multiple sensors may select the same channel, making it difficult to directly identify which sensor transmitted which information. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a Mobile Data Gathering Station (MDGS) (Fig. 1(b)). The MDGS traverses multiple aggregation points, broadcasts a request signal at each point, and collects PhyC-SN responses from sensors within its coverage. At each aggregation point, the system records the candidate sensors that could have responded and the channels that were actually observed (Fig. 1(c)). The key idea of the proposed method is to identify the correspondence between individual sensors and their channels by cross-referencing records from multiple aggre-gation points (Fig. 1(d)). For example, if a sensor could respond at both Point 1 and Point 2, and only one channel is commonly observed at both points, then that sensor’s transmitted channel can be uniquely identified. This paper designs a database update algorithm that performs such cross-referencing efficiently and robustly, achieving high-accuracy sensor information identification even in the presence of missing data and estimation errors. The details of PhyC-SN are described in Section IV, the observation procedure and record format using MDGS in Section V, and the proposed algorithm in Section VI.

A. OVERVIEW OF MDGS

The MDGS broadcasts a request signal, and the sensors respond by transmitting an unmodulated carrier at a frequency corresponding to their observed (quantized) infor-mation. ## Abstract:

This paper is concerned with the application of wireless sensor network (WSN) technology to long-duration and large-scale environmental monitoring. The holy grail is a system that can be deployed and operated by domain specialists not engineers, but this remains some distance into the future. We present our views as to why this field has progressed less quickly than many envisaged it would over a decade ago. We use real examples taken from our own work in this field to illustrate the technological difficulties and challenges that are entailed in meeting end-user requirements for information gathering systems. Reliability and productivity are key concerns and influence the design choices for system hardware and software. We conclude with a discussion of long-term challenges for WSN technology in environmental monitoring and outline our vision of the future.

ICEMI 2007 

# Wireless Sensor Network Based on IEEE 1451.0 and 

# IEEE 1451.5-802.11 

Kang Lee, Eugene Song 

National Institute of Standards and Technology 

100 Bureau Drive, MS# 8220 

Gaithersburg, Maryland USA 20899-8220 

E-Mail:  kang.lee@nist.gov , ysong@nist.gov 

Abstract - This paper describes a wireless sensor network (WSN) based on the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)’s 1451.0, 1451.5, and 802.11 standards. The implementation of the IEEE-based WSN was developed at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The WSN consists of two wireless nodes - the Network Capable Application Processor (NCAP) node and the Wireless Transducer Interface Module (WTIM) node. In operation the NCAP node communicates wirelessly with the WTIM node using the IEEE 1451.0 and IEEE 1451.5 interfaces through the IEEE 802.11 wireless communication modules. In the paper two case studies illustrate the implementation of the request and response of the sensor data and Transducer Electronic Data Sheet (TEDS) using the client-server model. The work described provides afoundation and some guidelines for implementing a wireless sensor monitoring application based on the IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5 standards. 

Keywords - IEEE 1451.0; IEEE 1451.5; NCAP; WTIM; TIM; TEDS; sensors interface; sensor standard; smart transducer; wireless sensor network; IEEE 802.11 

1 Introduction 

The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Instrumentation and Measurement Society’s Technical Committee on Sensor Technology has developed a family of Smart Transducer Interface Standards called IEEE 1451. The standards define a set of open, common, network-independent communication interfaces for connecting transducers (defined as sensors or actuators) to microprocessors, instruments, and control/field networks [1]. The IEEE 1451 family provides a set of protocols for wired and wireless distributed sensor applications. Figure 1 shows the architecture for the suite of IEEE 1451 standards. According to the architecture, IEEE 1451 defines a Transducer Interface Module (TIM) and Network Capable Application Processor (NCAP). The TIM can be a wired or wireless IEEE 1451.X module consisting of up to 255 transducers, signal conversion and processing electronics, and Transducer Electronic Data Sheets (TEDS). The TEDS provide transducer ID (identification), measurement range, location, calibration and user information, and more. The NCAP can access the TIM and pass the transducer information to the network. There are three possible ways to access the sensors and actuators from a network: IEEE 1451.1, IEEE 1451.0 Hyper Text Transfer Protocol (HTTP), and a proposed Smart Transducer Web Services (STWS) [2].

The IEEE 1451.0 standard defines a set of common functionality, commands, and TEDS for the IEEE 1451 family. This functionality is independent of the physical communications media. It includes the basic functions for the NCAP to read and write to each transducer and its TEDS, and to send configuration, control, and operation commands to the TIM. The STWS allow direct network access to the TIM through IEEE 1451.0 using web services. Through a communication interface module, IEEE 1451.0 can talk to the IEEE 1451.X on the NCAP. The IEEE 1451.X on the NCAP can talk to the IEEE 1451.X on the TIM through the IEEE 1451.X physical interfaces. This interface provides a means for interoperability between the communication modules of the NCAP and TIM. The IEEE 1451.X refers to a physical interface, which is a device or part of a device that is in compliance with IEEE Std. 1451.2-1997 [3, 4], IEEE Std. 1451.3-2003, or IEEE 1451.5 (IEEE 802.11, Bluetooth, and ZigBee)**, etc. The main goal of IEEE 1451.0 is to enable the access of transducer data through a common set of interfaces whether the transducers are connected to systems or networks via wired or wireless means. 2 Related Work 

Recent advances in wireless communications and electronics have enabled the development of small (in size), low-cost, low-power, and multifunctional sensor nodes that can communicate over short distances. Smart, wireless, networked sensors will become more widely used, collectively processing vast amounts of previously unrecorded data to help monitor the condition of the environment, machining systems, and other applications. Standardized transducer interfaces, high-level programming languages, and wireless network technologies are serving to shape the next-generation, wireless monitoring landscape. The first Wireless Sensing Workshop was held in June 2001 at the Sensors Expo/Conference in Chicago, Illinois. The need for astandard protocol for wireless sensor networks (WSN) was echoed. A suggestion was made to create a wireless sensor interface standard IEEE 1451.5 and to use the IEEE 802 family as a guideline for managing the IEEE 1451 framework [5]. Consequently the first draft of IEEE 1451.5 was introduced at the 2004 Sensors Expo/Conference. Through the vigorous standardization effort, the IEEE 1451.5 draft was finally approved as an IEEE-SA (Standards Association) standard in March 2007 [6]. A modular approach to the development of IEEE 1451.5 wireless sensors based on Bluetooth is discussed in reference [7]. An implementation of IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5 is presented in reference [8]. 

3 Architecture of IEEE 1451 Wireless Sensor Network 

3.1 Architecture 

Figure 2 shows the architecture of the IEEE 1451 WSN. The NCAP is a device that could contain one or more wireless radios based on 802.11, Bluetooth, or ZigBee. It can talk to one or more Wireless Transducer Interface Module (WTIM). Each WTIM contains the corresponding radio(s) matching those in the NCAP, along with the other components of a TIM.

3.2 IEEE 1451.0 Standard 

The IEEE 1451.0, approved as an IEEE standard on March 23, 2007, defines a set of common operations and TEDS for the IEEE 1451 family. It aims to facilitate interoperability and compatibility among the suite of IEEE 1451 standards. Since the functionality defined in IEEE 1451.0 is independent of the physical communications media between the transducers and NCAP, it is easy to add other proposed IEEE 1451.X physical layers to the family [9, 10]. The IEEE 1451.0 TransducerServices 

contain methods to read and write transducer channels, read and write TEDS, and send configuration, control, and operation commands to the TIMs. The 

ModuleCommunication Interface between IEEE 1451.0 and IEEE 1451.X contains three interfaces: Comm ,

Receive , and Registration . The Comm interface can be divided into NetComm and P2PComm interface. The 

ModuleCommunication Interface is a symmetric interface that is implemented on both the NCAP and TIM sides. 

3.3 IEEE 1451.5 Standard 

The IEEE 1451.5 standard is a wireless sensor interface standard, which defines a set of wireless communication specifications between the WTIM and NCAP. It adopts popular 802.11, Bluetooth, and ZigBee as its wireless communication protocols. It could accept other wireless protocols such as ultra-wide band, as needed. Through the NCAP, sensor information can be made available for network and web access. The IEEE 802.11 radio specification for the IEEE 1451.5 provides adescription of the functions, protocols, and interfaces that are to be performed by the 802.11 communication module between the WTIM and the NCAP. 

4 Implementation of IEEE 1451 WSN 

4.1 WSN Based on IEEE 1451 

Figure 3 shows the implementation of a WSN based on IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5-802.11 using IEEE 1451.2 sensors. This WSN consists of one NCAP node and one WTIM node. An IEEE 1451.2 sensor is connected to the WTIM via a serial port. The NCAP can communicate wirelessly with WTIM through IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5 protocols using the client-server and publisher-subscriber communication models. The client-server and publisher-subscriber communications between the two nodes can be implemented using Transmission Control Protocol /Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) and Transmission Control Protocol / User Datagram Protocol (TCP/UDP), respectively. 5 Case Studies 

IEEE 1451.2 sensor data and TEDS reading are taken as case studies to test the implementation of the IEEE 1451 WSN. When a WTIM starts up, the communication module of the TIM first registers to the TIM; second, the TIM initiates a TIMAnnouncement to the NCAP. Then the NCAP follows with a TIMDiscovery. The detailed information for TIMAnnouncement and TIMDiscovery can be found in reference 2. The two case studies are described in the following sections. The wireless communications between the NCAP and WTIM are implemented through 

NetTwoWayClient and NetTwoWayServer help classes .ICEMI 2007 

5.1 Case 1: Request-Response of Sensor Data 

Figure 6 shows some sensor readings on a user interface. The NCAP sends the WTIM a request to read sensor data on transducer channel 2 of the IEEE 1451.2 device. When the WTIM receives the request, it reads the sensor data via a serial port and sends the data to the NCAP. The value and status of the transducer channel 2, in this case, an illumination reading of 11, is shown in Figure 6.

5.2 Case 2: Request-Response of MetaID TEDS 

Figure 7 shows the user interfaces and results of TEDS reading. The NCAP sends the WTIM a request to read the 1451.2 MetaID TEDS. When the WTIM receives the request from the NCAP, it reads the MetaID TEDS via the serial port and returns the sensor TEDS to the NCAP. 

6 Conclusions 

This paper describes a wireless sensor network based on the IEEE 1451.0 and IEEE 1451.5-802.11 wireless sensor standards. The wireless sensor network consists of two wireless nodes, the Network Capable Application Processor (NCAP) node and the Wireless Transducer Interface Module (STIM) node. The NCAP communicates wirelessly with the WTIM adhering to the IEEE 1451.0 and IEEE 1451.5 standards using the 802.11 wireless communication modules. Two example cases were discussed and used to illustrate the communications of sensor data and Transducer Electronic Data Sheets (TEDS) data using the client-server model. The work described in this paper provides a foundation for implementing wireless sensor applications based on the IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5 standards. Our future work will involve the implementation and application of wireless sensor networks based on IEEE 1451.5 for manufacturing systems.

Brief Bio 

Kang Lee received his BSEE and MSEE from the Johns Hopkins University and University of Maryland, respectively. Kang is the Leader of Sensor Development and Application Group at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). He is responsible for R&D in smart sensor networking, distributed measurement and control systems, and sensor-RFID integration. Kang is the Chairman of the IEEE Instrumentation and Measurement Society’s Technical Committee on Sensor Technology and responsible for the establishment of the suite of IEEE 1451 smart sensor communication and interface standards. 

Eugene Song received his Ph.D. from the Tsinghua University, Beijing. Eugene is a guest researcher at NIST. He was a professor at Hebei Institute of Technology, P. R. China. He has published over 50 technical papers. His current research interests include networked smart sensor interfaces, IEEE 1451 smart transducer standards, and distributed measurement and control systems.

ICEMI 2007 

# Wireless Sensor Network Based on IEEE 1451.0 and 

# IEEE 1451.5-802.11 

Kang Lee, Eugene Song 

National Institute of Standards and Technology 

100 Bureau Drive, MS# 8220 

Gaithersburg, Maryland USA 20899-8220 

E-Mail:  kang.lee@nist.gov , ysong@nist.gov 

Abstract - This paper describes a wireless sensor network (WSN) based on the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)’s 1451.0, 1451.5, and 802.11 standards. The implementation of the IEEE-based WSN was developed at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The WSN consists of two wireless nodes - the Network Capable Application Processor (NCAP) node and the Wireless Transducer Interface Module (WTIM) node. In operation the NCAP node communicates wirelessly with the WTIM node using the IEEE 1451.0 and IEEE 1451.5 interfaces through the IEEE 802.11 wireless communication modules. In the paper two case studies illustrate the implementation of the request and response of the sensor data and Transducer Electronic Data Sheet (TEDS) using the client-server model. The work described provides afoundation and some guidelines for implementing a wireless sensor monitoring application based on the IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5 standards. 

Keywords - IEEE 1451.0; IEEE 1451.5; NCAP; WTIM; TIM; TEDS; sensors interface; sensor standard; smart transducer; wireless sensor network; IEEE 802.11 

1 Introduction 

The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Instrumentation and Measurement Society’s Technical Committee on Sensor Technology has developed a family of Smart Transducer Interface Standards called IEEE 1451. The standards define a set of open, common, network-independent communication interfaces for connecting transducers (defined as sensors or actuators) to microprocessors, instruments, and control/field networks [1]. The IEEE 1451 family provides a set of protocols for wired and wireless distributed sensor applications. Figure 1 shows the architecture for the suite of IEEE 1451 standards. According to the architecture, IEEE 1451 defines a Transducer Interface Module (TIM) and Network Capable Application Processor (NCAP). The TIM can be a wired or wireless IEEE 1451.X module consisting of up to 255 transducers, signal conversion and processing electronics, and Transducer Electronic Data Sheets (TEDS). The TEDS provide transducer ID (identification), measurement range, location, calibration and user information, and more. The NCAP can access the TIM and pass the transducer information to the network. There are three possible ways to access the sensors and actuators from a network: IEEE 1451.1, IEEE 1451.0 Hyper Text Transfer Protocol (HTTP), and a proposed Smart Transducer Web Services (STWS) [2].

The IEEE 1451.0 standard defines a set of common functionality, commands, and TEDS for the IEEE 1451 family. This functionality is independent of the physical communications media. It includes the basic functions for the NCAP to read and write to each transducer and its TEDS, and to send configuration, control, and operation commands to the TIM. The STWS allow direct network access to the TIM through IEEE 1451.0 using web services. Through a communication interface module, IEEE 1451.0 can talk to the IEEE 1451.X on the NCAP. The IEEE 1451.X on the NCAP can talk to the IEEE 1451.X on the TIM through the IEEE 1451.X physical interfaces. This interface provides a means for interoperability between the communication modules of the NCAP and TIM. The IEEE 1451.X refers to a physical interface, which is a device or part of a device that is in compliance with IEEE Std. 1451.2-1997 [3, 4], IEEE Std. 1451.3-2003, or IEEE 1451.5 (IEEE 802.11, Bluetooth, and ZigBee)**, etc. The main goal of IEEE 1451.0 is to enable the access of transducer data through a common set of interfaces whether the transducers are connected to systems or networks via wired or wireless means. 2 Related Work 

Recent advances in wireless communications and electronics have enabled the development of small (in size), low-cost, low-power, and multifunctional sensor nodes that can communicate over short distances. Smart, wireless, networked sensors will become more widely used, collectively processing vast amounts of previously unrecorded data to help monitor the condition of the environment, machining systems, and other applications. Standardized transducer interfaces, high-level programming languages, and wireless network technologies are serving to shape the next-generation, wireless monitoring landscape. The first Wireless Sensing Workshop was held in June 2001 at the Sensors Expo/Conference in Chicago, Illinois. The need for astandard protocol for wireless sensor networks (WSN) was echoed. A suggestion was made to create a wireless sensor interface standard IEEE 1451.5 and to use the IEEE 802 family as a guideline for managing the IEEE 1451 framework [5]. Consequently the first draft of IEEE 1451.5 was introduced at the 2004 Sensors Expo/Conference. Through the vigorous standardization effort, the IEEE 1451.5 draft was finally approved as an IEEE-SA (Standards Association) standard in March 2007 [6]. A modular approach to the development of IEEE 1451.5 wireless sensors based on Bluetooth is discussed in reference [7]. An implementation of IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5 is presented in reference [8]. 

3 Architecture of IEEE 1451 Wireless Sensor Network 

3.1 Architecture 

Figure 2 shows the architecture of the IEEE 1451 WSN. The NCAP is a device that could contain one or more wireless radios based on 802.11, Bluetooth, or ZigBee. It can talk to one or more Wireless Transducer Interface Module (WTIM). Each WTIM contains the corresponding radio(s) matching those in the NCAP, along with the other components of a TIM.

3.2 IEEE 1451.0 Standard 

The IEEE 1451.0, approved as an IEEE standard on March 23, 2007, defines a set of common operations and TEDS for the IEEE 1451 family. It aims to facilitate interoperability and compatibility among the suite of IEEE 1451 standards. Since the functionality defined in IEEE 1451.0 is independent of the physical communications media between the transducers and NCAP, it is easy to add other proposed IEEE 1451.X physical layers to the family [9, 10]. The IEEE 1451.0 TransducerServices 

contain methods to read and write transducer channels, read and write TEDS, and send configuration, control, and operation commands to the TIMs. The 

ModuleCommunication Interface between IEEE 1451.0 and IEEE 1451.X contains three interfaces: Comm ,

Receive , and Registration . The Comm interface can be divided into NetComm and P2PComm interface. The 

ModuleCommunication Interface is a symmetric interface that is implemented on both the NCAP and TIM sides. 

3.3 IEEE 1451.5 Standard 

The IEEE 1451.5 standard is a wireless sensor interface standard, which defines a set of wireless communication specifications between the WTIM and NCAP. It adopts popular 802.11, Bluetooth, and ZigBee as its wireless communication protocols. It could accept other wireless protocols such as ultra-wide band, as needed. Through the NCAP, sensor information can be made available for network and web access. The IEEE 802.11 radio specification for the IEEE 1451.5 provides adescription of the functions, protocols, and interfaces that are to be performed by the 802.11 communication module between the WTIM and the NCAP. 

4 Implementation of IEEE 1451 WSN 

4.1 WSN Based on IEEE 1451 

Figure 3 shows the implementation of a WSN based on IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5-802.11 using IEEE 1451.2 sensors. This WSN consists of one NCAP node and one WTIM node. An IEEE 1451.2 sensor is connected to the WTIM via a serial port. The NCAP can communicate wirelessly with WTIM through IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5 protocols using the client-server and publisher-subscriber communication models. The client-server and publisher-subscriber communications between the two nodes can be implemented using Transmission Control Protocol /Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) and Transmission Control Protocol / User Datagram Protocol (TCP/UDP), respectively. 5 Case Studies 

IEEE 1451.2 sensor data and TEDS reading are taken as case studies to test the implementation of the IEEE 1451 WSN. When a WTIM starts up, the communication module of the TIM first registers to the TIM; second, the TIM initiates a TIMAnnouncement to the NCAP. Then the NCAP follows with a TIMDiscovery. The detailed information for TIMAnnouncement and TIMDiscovery can be found in reference 2. The two case studies are described in the following sections. The wireless communications between the NCAP and WTIM are implemented through 

NetTwoWayClient and NetTwoWayServer help classes .ICEMI 2007 

5.1 Case 1: Request-Response of Sensor Data 

Figure 6 shows some sensor readings on a user interface. The NCAP sends the WTIM a request to read sensor data on transducer channel 2 of the IEEE 1451.2 device. When the WTIM receives the request, it reads the sensor data via a serial port and sends the data to the NCAP. The value and status of the transducer channel 2, in this case, an illumination reading of 11, is shown in Figure 6. 

Figure 6. Request-Response of sensor data 

Figure 7. Request-Response MetaID TEDS 

5.2 Case 2: Request-Response of MetaID TEDS 

Figure 7 shows the user interfaces and results of TEDS reading. The NCAP sends the WTIM a request to read the 1451.2 MetaID TEDS. When the WTIM receives the request from the NCAP, it reads the MetaID TEDS via the serial port and returns the sensor TEDS to the NCAP. 

6 Conclusions 

This paper describes a wireless sensor network based on the IEEE 1451.0 and IEEE 1451.5-802.11 wireless sensor standards. The wireless sensor network consists of two wireless nodes, the Network Capable Application Processor (NCAP) node and the Wireless Transducer Interface Module (STIM) node. The NCAP communicates wirelessly with the WTIM adhering to the IEEE 1451.0 and IEEE 1451.5 standards using the 802.11 wireless communication modules. Two example cases were discussed and used to illustrate the communications of sensor data and Transducer Electronic Data Sheets (TEDS) data using the client-server model. The work described in this paper provides a foundation for implementing wireless sensor applications based on the IEEE 1451.0 and 1451.5 standards. Our future work will involve the implementation and application of wireless sensor networks based on IEEE 1451.5 for manufacturing systems.

## Abstract

Wireless ad hoc sensor networks have the potential to provide the missing interface between the physical world and the Internet, thus impacting a large number of users. This connection will enable computational treatments of the physical world in ways never before possible. In this far reaching scenario, Quality of Service can be expressed in terms of accuracy and/or latency of observing events and the overall state of the physical world. Consequently, one of the fundamental problems in sensor networks is the calculation of coverage, which can be defined as a measure of the ability to detect objects within a sensor filed. Exposure is directly related to coverage in that it is an integral measure of how well the sensor network can observe an object, moving on an arbitrary path, over a period of time. After elucidating the importance of exposure, we formally define exposure and study its properties. We have developed an efficient and effective algorithm for exposure calculations in sensor networks, specifically for finding minimal exposure paths. The minimal exposure path provides valuable information about the worst case exposure-based coverage in sensor networks. The algorithm can be applied to any given distribution of sensors, sensor and sensitivity models, and characteristics of the network. Furthermore, it provides an unbounded level of accuracy as a function of run time and storage. Finally, we provide an extensive collection of experimental results and study the scaling behavior of exposure and the proposed algorithm for its calculation.

## Abstract

Wireless ad hoc sensor networks have the potential to provide the missing interface between the physical world and the Internet, thus impacting a large number of users. This connection will enable computational treatments of the physical world in ways never before possible. In this far reaching scenario, Quality of Service can be expressed in terms of accuracy and/or latency of observing events and the overall state of the physical world. Consequently, one of the fundamental problems in sensor networks is the calculation of coverage, which can be defined as a measure of the ability to detect objects within a sensor filed. Exposure is directly related to coverage in that it is an integral measure of how well the sensor network can observe an object, moving on an arbitrary path, over a period of time. After elucidating the importance of exposure, we formally define exposure and study its properties. We have developed an efficient and effective algorithm for exposure calculations in sensor networks, specifically for finding minimal exposure paths. The minimal exposure path provides valuable information about the worst case exposure-based coverage in sensor networks. The algorithm can be applied to any given distribution of sensors, sensor and sensitivity models, and characteristics of the network. Furthermore, it provides an unbounded level of accuracy as a function of run time and storage. Finally, we provide an extensive collection of experimental results and study the scaling behavior of exposure and the proposed algorithm for its calculation.

# National Academy of Engineering Elects 111 Members and 22 International Members

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Wed, February 09, 2022

Washington, D.C., February 09, 2022 —
The National Academy of Engineering (NAE) has elected 111 new members and 22 international members, announced NAE President John L. Anderson today. This brings the total U.S. membership to 2,388 and the number of international members to 310.

Election to the National Academy of Engineering is among the highest professional distinctions accorded to an engineer. Academy membership honors those who have made outstanding contributions to "engineering research, practice, or education, including, where appropriate, significant contributions to the engineering literature" and to "the pioneering of new and developing fields of technology, making major advancements in traditional fields of engineering, or developing/implementing innovative approaches to engineering education." Election of new NAE members is the culmination of a yearlong process. The ballot is set in December and the final vote for membership occurs during January.

Individuals in the newly elected class will be formally inducted during the NAE's annual meeting on Oct. 2, 2022. A list of the new members and international members follows, with their primary affiliations at the time of election and a brief statement of their principal engineering accomplishments.

# New Members:

**Abdelrazaq, Ahmad,**former senior executive vice president, Samsung C&T Corp., Seongnam, South Korea. For innovation in design, construction, and health monitoring of the world's tallest and most complex building structures.

**Afeyan, Noubar B.,**co-founder and chairman, Moderna Inc., Cambridge, Mass. For leadership in biotechnology, in particular mRNA therapeutics and chromatography.

**Arbige, Michael V.,**executive vice president (retired), DuPont Nutrition & BioSciences, Montara, Calif. For leadership in developing and commercializing engineered enzyme products with industrial, consumer, and sustainability benefits.

**Argrow, Brian M.,**professor and chair, Ann and H.J. Smead Aerospace Engineering Sciences, University of Colorado, Boulder. For contributions to unmanned aerial systems capable of penetrating severe storms and leadership in their application to scientific observation.

**Aung, MiMi A.,**senior manager, Project Kuiper, Kuiper Systems LLC, Bellevue, Wash. For development of the NASA Mars Helicopter and the first flight on another planet.

**Balazs, Anna Christina,**John A. Swanson Chair, Swanson School of Engineering, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh. For creative and imaginative work in predicting the behavior of soft materials that are composed of multiple cooperatively - interacting components.

**Baraniuk, Richard G.,**C. Sidney Burrus Professor, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Rice University, Houston. For the development and broad dissemination of open educational resources and for foundational contributions to compressive sensing.

**Bergeron, Kathleen,**vice president, Hardware Engineering, Apple Inc., Los Gatos, Calif. For contributions to and leadership in the invention and engineering product realization of innovative designs.

**Bizios, Rena,**Lutcher Brown Endowed Chair Professor, Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of Texas, San Antonio. For contributions to the theory and applications of cellular tissue engineering, cell/biomaterial interactions, and surface modification biomaterials.

**Bovik, Alan C.,**Cockrell Family Regents Endowed Chair in Engineering and professor, Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Texas, Austin. For contributions to the development of tools for image and video quality assessment.

**Bridges, Charles R.,**Executive Vice President & Chief Scientific Officer at CorVista Health, Inc.. For leading the industrial development of new engineered device treatments in the cardiopulmonary space and for pharmaceutical innovation.

**Cao, Jian,**Cardiss Collins Professor, McCormick School of Engineering, Northwestern University, Evanston, Ill. For pioneering a flexible sheet forming system and for leadership in manufacturing.

**Carter, Paul J.,**Genentech Fellow, Antibody Engineering, Genentech Inc., San Francisco. For creating novel approaches to discovering and developing life-saving antibody therapeutics, including bispecific antibodies.

**Clark, Robert L., Jr.,**professor, Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Rochester, Rochester, N.Y. For development of automated tools for rapidly identifying and indexing desirable genetic traits for next-generation seed and biotechnology product development.

**Clayton, Norma B.,**vice president (retired), Learning, Training, and Development, Boeing Co., St. Charles, Mo. For leadership in transforming manufacturing processes and supply chain management, and for innovative training programs for commercial aerospace industries.

**Cohn, John Maxwell,**IBM Fellow, MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab, Cambridge, Mass. For improving design productivity of high-performance analog and mixed-signal circuits and for evangelizing STEM education.

**Croak, Marian R.,**vice president, Engineering, Google LLC, Fair Haven, N.J. For technical and managerial leadership in the implementation of packet voice networking and for promotion of minority inclusion in engineering.

**Czerwinski, Mary,**partner researcher and research manager, Microsoft Research, Redmond, Wash. For the application of psychological principles to the design and understanding of human computer interaction.

**Davies, John,**vice president (retired), World Ahead, Intel Corp., Sonoma, Calif. For contributions in computer technology to improve education and health care, stimulate economies, and enrich lives throughout underdeveloped countries.

**De Yoreo, James J.,**chief scientist, Physical Sciences Division, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Richland, Wash. For advances in materials synthesis from nucleation to large-scale crystal growth.
